title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
text:
A multiplex cytokine panel measures dozens of analytes in every sample. The tempting analysis is quick: run a t-test on each cytokine, put a star on everything below 0.05, and write up the stars. But cytokine data breaks the assumptions behind that approach in several ways at once, and the result can both miss real effects and report false ones.
This article works through seven decisions that change the answer, using a simulated dataset where the truth is known, because the effects were built into it.
Show the code: packages and data
library(readxl)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)
library(kableExtra)
library(here)

# Every table in the article goes through this, so they share one style
show_table <- function(x, ...) {
  kbl(x, ...) |>
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                  full_width = FALSE, position = "left")
}

plasma_raw <- read_excel(here("tutorials", "data", "bal_plasma_cytokines.xlsx"),
                         sheet = "Plasma", col_types = "text")
metadata <- read_csv(here("tutorials", "data", "bal_metadata_clean.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

cytokines <- setdiff(names(plasma_raw), c("Pt_ID", "Visit", "Notes"))

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
teal <- "#0F4C5C"
orange <- "#E36414"

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
section: 1. Read what the assay actually reported
text:
1. Read what the assay actually reported
Open a multiplex export and many cells aren’t numbers. Each cytokine has a range the assay can measure. Values below the lower limit come back as codes such as OOR <4.8 (“out of range, below 4.8 pg/ml”), and values above the upper limit as OOR >30432.0. The same code is often written several ways in one file:


Show the code
plasma_raw |>
  select(Pt_ID, Visit, `IL-10`, `IL-13`, `GM-CSF`) |>
  filter(if_all(c(`IL-10`, `IL-13`, `GM-CSF`), \(x) str_detect(x, "<"))) |>
  head(4) |>
  show_table()

Before choosing any test, turn the codes into information instead of throwing them away. For each value, record whether it was below or above the limit, and what the limit was:


Show the code: parse the out-of-range codes
plasma <- plasma_raw |>
  mutate(Pt_ID = toupper(Pt_ID)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(cytokines), names_to = "cytokine", values_to = "reported") |>
  mutate(
    below = str_detect(reported, "<"),
    above = str_detect(reported, ">"),
    limit = as.numeric(str_extract(reported, "[0-9.]+$")),
    value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(reported))
  ) |>
  inner_join(select(metadata, pt_id, tb_diagnosis, hiv_status), by = c("Pt_ID" = "pt_id"))

# Each cytokine's lower limit of detection, taken from its own codes
lod <- plasma |> filter(below) |> distinct(cytokine, lod = limit)

plasma <- plasma |>
  left_join(lod, by = "cytokine") |>
  mutate(cytokine = factor(cytokine, levels = cytokines))




Show the code: share below the limit
plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline") |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(below = mean(below) * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(below, reorder(cytokine, below))) +
  geom_col(fill = teal) +
  labs(x = "Below the detection limit (%)", y = NULL)








Figure 1: Share of baseline samples below the lower limit of detection, by cytokine (simulated data).





In this dataset, between 0% and 35% of baseline values fall below the limit, depending on the cytokine (Figure 1). That’s too many to ignore.

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
section: 2. Think twice before dropping values below the detection limit
text:
2. Think twice before dropping values below the detection limit
The easiest thing to do with OOR <4.8 is to treat it as missing. It can also do the most damage. A value below the limit isn’t entirely unknown: we know it’s low. Dropping it removes exactly the low values, and if one group has more of them, it removes the difference you’re looking for.
IL-10 shows how much this matters. The simulation includes a real increase in IL-10 in the active TB group. Compare the four diagnosis groups at baseline with a Kruskal-Wallis test, first dropping the values below the limit, then keeping them:


Show the code: IL-10, dropped vs kept
il10 <- plasma |> filter(Visit == "Baseline", cytokine == "IL-10")

# 1. Below-limit values treated as missing (dropped)
dropped <- kruskal.test(value ~ tb_diagnosis, data = il10)

# 2. Below-limit values kept as the lowest values
kept <- kruskal.test(if_else(below, 0, value) ~ tb_diagnosis, data = il10)

tibble(
  approach = c("Below-limit values dropped", "Below-limit values kept as lowest"),
  p_value  = format.pval(c(dropped$p.value, kept$p.value), digits = 2)
) |>
  show_table(col.names = c("Approach", "Kruskal-Wallis p"), align = "lr")

  group_by(tb_diagnosis) |>
  summarise(n = n(), detected = round(mean(!below) * 100)) |>
  show_table(col.names = c("Diagnosis", "Samples", "Detected (%)"))

IL-10 was detected in 85% of the active TB group but only 68% of controls (Table 3). Dropping the undetected values throws away that difference.
If you keep them, the options depend on how many values are below the limit and which method you use:

Rank-based tests (Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis) handle it neatly. Every value below the limit is smaller than every detected value, so they all tie for the lowest ranks. It doesn’t matter what number you put in for them, as long as it’s below the limit: the test gives the same answer. That’s why replacing them with 0 above works.
Simple substitution with the limit divided by √2 or by 2 is common when you need means or fold changes. Hornung and Reed suggested the limit ÷ √2 for data that isn’t highly skewed, and the limit ÷ 2 when it is (Hornung and Reed, 1990).
Methods designed for censored data are more principled. Substituting a value and then running t-tests has repeatedly been shown to give inaccurate results, and survival-analysis methods built for “less than” values avoid the guess altogether (Helsel, 2012). Multiple imputation is another option: each value below the limit is filled in several times with plausible values below the limit, and the results are combined so the uncertainty about the true values is carried into the analysis. In simulations with 10% to 60% of values below the limit, it gave less biased estimates than substitution, particularly as the share below the limit grew (Zhang and Guo, 2012).
When most values are below the limit, the concentration carries little information. Analyse whether the cytokine was detected or not instead, with a chi-square or Fisher’s exact test.

What I’m doing in my master’s. My master’s analysis, which is still under way, takes a different approach. First, I leave out any cytokine with more than 40–50% of its values out of range or missing, because so little of it has actually been measured. Then, for the cytokines I keep, I leave the OOR values out of the tests and don’t substitute anything for them. The true values aren’t known, and I don’t want a guessed number to skew the results.
This is one approach among several, and it isn’t universally accepted. Each choice has a cost: leaving the values out can hide a real difference, as IL-10 shows above, while substituting a value means analysing a number nobody measured. Section 5 runs the whole panel both ways, so you can see what the choice changes.


Show the code: apply a 40% cutoff
oor_share <- plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline") |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(pct_oor = mean(below | above | is.na(reported)) * 100, .groups = "drop")

excluded <- oor_share |> filter(pct_oor > 40)


In this dataset a 40% cutoff removes nothing: the cytokine with the most OOR values, IL-13, has 35% at baseline.
Values above the upper limit are rarer. Set them to the upper limit, and note how many there were.
The rest of this article keeps every value: ranks for testing, and the limit ÷ √2 where a number is needed.


Show the code: substitute the limit ÷ √2
plasma <- plasma |>
  mutate(conc = case_when(
    below ~ lod / sqrt(2),
    above ~ limit,
    TRUE  ~ value
  ))

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
section: 3. Expect skewed concentrations, and log them
text:
3. Expect skewed concentrations, and log them
Cytokine concentrations in this dataset have a long right tail: most samples are low, a few are very high. IP-10 is typical (Figure 2):


Show the code: histograms of IP-10
plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline", cytokine == "IP-10") |>
  transmute(`pg/ml` = conc, `log(pg/ml)` = log(conc)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, levels = c("pg/ml", "log(pg/ml)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = teal, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Samples")








Figure 2: Baseline IP-10 in pg/ml (left) and on a log scale (right). The log-transformed values are close to symmetric (simulated data).





The histogram is the first check. The second is a formal test of normality, the Shapiro-Wilk test, whose null hypothesis is that the values come from a normal distribution: a small p-value means they probably don’t.


Show the code: Shapiro-Wilk test on IP-10
ip10 <- plasma |> filter(Visit == "Baseline", cytokine == "IP-10")
tibble(
  scale = c("Original (pg/ml)", "Logged"),
  p     = format.pval(c(shapiro.test(ip10$conc)$p.value,
                        shapiro.test(log(ip10$conc))$p.value), digits = 2)
) |>
  show_table(col.names = c("Scale", "Shapiro-Wilk p"), align = "lr")




Table 4: Shapiro-Wilk test of baseline IP-10 on the original and log scales (simulated data).

Shapiro-Wilk p

On the original scale, a t-test’s assumption of roughly normal values fails badly (Shapiro-Wilk p < 0.001; Table 4). After a log transformation the values are close to normal (p = 0.25), and the parametric tests are back on the table (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.24.4).
IP-10 is one of the easy cases, though. Run the same test on every cytokine:


Show the code: Shapiro-Wilk test on all 27 cytokines
normality <- plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline") |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(
    pct_below = mean(below) * 100,
    p_original = shapiro.test(conc)$p.value,
    p_logged   = shapiro.test(log(conc))$p.value,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

normality |>
  mutate(values_below_limit = case_when(
    pct_below == 0 ~ "None",
    pct_below < 1  ~ "Under 1%",
    TRUE           ~ "1% or more"
  ),
  values_below_limit = factor(values_below_limit, levels = c("None", "Under 1%", "1% or more"))) |>
  group_by(values_below_limit) |>
  summarise(cytokines = n(),
            normal_original = sum(p_original > 0.05),
            normal_logged   = sum(p_logged > 0.05)) |>
  arrange(values_below_limit) |>
  show_table(col.names = c("Values below the limit", "Cytokines",
                           "Normal, original scale", "Normal, logged"))

None of the 27 cytokines look normal on the original scale (Table 5). After logging, 15 do: the 12 with no values below the detection limit, and 3 with only one or two. The other 12, each with 5% or more of its values below the limit, still fail after logging, and the histogram shows why. IL-13, the cytokine with the most values below the limit, has a spike where every substituted value sits at the same number (Figure 3):


Show the code: histogram of logged IL-13
plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline", cytokine == "IL-13") |>
  ggplot(aes(log(conc))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = teal, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "log(pg/ml)", y = "Samples")








Figure 3: Baseline IL-13 on a log scale. The spike on the left is the 35% of samples below the detection limit, all substituted with the same value (simulated data).





No transformation can spread out values that were all given the same number, and leaving them out doesn’t help either: the detected values alone stop sharply at the limit. For cytokines with values below the limit, rank-based tests are the safer route.
Use the histogram and the test together. With hundreds of samples, Shapiro-Wilk can flag departures from normality too small to matter; with a handful, it can miss large ones. The picture shows what the p-value can’t: whether the problem is a long tail, a spike or a cut-off.
Logging also matches how cytokine differences are usually described: as ratios (“twice as high”) rather than differences in pg/ml. A t-test on log values compares geometric means, and its result transforms back into a ratio with a confidence interval (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.24.4). So there are two sound routes:

Log the values, then use t-tests or ANOVA, and report ratios.
Use rank-based tests on the original values, which need no transformation and handle the below-limit values automatically.

Running a t-test on the raw pg/ml values isn’t one of them.

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
section: 4. Match the test to the design
text:
4. Match the test to the design
Which test to use depends on the question, not the cytokine. My two-page guide to choosing a test and Tutorial 4 cover the choices in full; for cytokine panels, Table 6 sets out the common designs.



Table 6: Tests for common cytokine-panel designs, on logged values or on ranks.










Question
Logged values
Original values (ranks)




Two groups (active TB vs controls)
Welch’s t-test
Wilcoxon rank-sum


Three or more groups (all four diagnoses)
One-way ANOVA
Kruskal-Wallis


Same people at two visits
Paired t-test on the log differences
Wilcoxon signed-rank


Detected or not, by group
Chi-square, or Fisher’s exact for small counts
—






Repeated visits deserve particular care. The same participants were sampled at baseline, month 3 and month 6, so their samples aren’t independent. Comparing the visits as if they came from different people wastes the design. In the simulation, IP-10 falls during follow-up in the active TB group. Compare baseline with month 6 for the participants who have both:


Show the code: paired vs unpaired t-test
ip10_pairs <- plasma |>
  filter(cytokine == "IP-10", tb_diagnosis == "Active TB", Visit %in% c("Baseline", "Month6")) |>
  select(Pt_ID, Visit, conc) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Visit, values_from = conc) |>
  filter(!is.na(Baseline), !is.na(Month6))

log_change <- log(ip10_pairs$Month6) - log(ip10_pairs$Baseline)
paired   <- t.test(log_change)
unpaired <- t.test(log(ip10_pairs$Month6), log(ip10_pairs$Baseline))

tibble(
  participants = nrow(ip10_pairs),
  ratio        = round(exp(mean(log_change)), 2),
  ci_low       = round(exp(paired$conf.int[1]), 2),
  ci_high      = round(exp(paired$conf.int[2]), 2),
  p_paired     = format(signif(paired$p.value, 2)),
  p_unpaired   = format(signif(unpaired$p.value, 2))
) |>
  show_table(col.names = c("Participants", "Ratio (month 6 ÷ baseline)", "95% CI low",
                           "95% CI high", "p, paired", "p, unpaired"))

By month 6, IP-10 was on average 0.44 times its baseline level (95% CI 0.37 to 0.51; Table 7). The paired test’s p-value is about ten million times smaller than the unpaired one on the same data, because comparing each person with themselves removes the person-to-person variation (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.20.2).

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
text:
5. 27 cytokines means 27 tests
Each test at α = 0.05 has a 5% chance of a false positive. Run 27 of them on data with no real differences at all, and you’d expect more than one “significant” cytokine by chance alone (27 × 0.05 ≈ 1.4).
Compare active TB with controls at baseline, one Wilcoxon test per cytokine, then correct the p-values two ways:

Bonferroni multiplies each p-value by the number of tests. It strictly limits the chance of even one false positive, but it’s very cautious (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.5).
Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate: the expected proportion of false positives among the cytokines you call significant (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). It’s less cautious, which is why it’s widely used when many outcomes are tested at once.



Show the code: one Wilcoxon test per cytokine, then correct
screen <- plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline", tb_diagnosis %in% c("Active TB", "Control")) |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(
    ratio = exp(mean(log(conc[tb_diagnosis == "Active TB"])) -
                mean(log(conc[tb_diagnosis == "Control"]))),
    p = wilcox.test(conc ~ tb_diagnosis, exact = FALSE)$p.value,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    p_bonferroni = p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni"),
    q_bh         = p.adjust(p, method = "BH")
  ) |>
  arrange(p)

# p-values too small for the computer to store come out as 0; show them as "< 1e-16"
screen |>
  head(9) |>
  mutate(ratio = round(ratio, 2),
         across(c(p, p_bonferroni, q_bh), \(x) format.pval(x, digits = 2, eps = 1e-16))) |>
  show_table(col.names = c("Cytokine", "Ratio (active TB ÷ controls)", "p",
                           "p, Bonferroni", "q, Benjamini-Hochberg"))

Eight cytokines are significant before correction, and seven after either correction (Table 9). The one that drops out, Eotaxin (p = 0.03 in Table 8), is a cytokine with no effect in the simulation: a false positive that the uncorrected analysis would have reported as a finding. The seven that survive are exactly the seven with a built-in difference.
Correction doesn’t make a panel foolproof. The false discovery rate is controlled on average, so some false positives can still get through, and every correction trades some power for fewer false alarms. But reporting uncorrected p-values from 27 tests reports noise as findings.

The same screen with the OOR values left out
Here is the analysis from Table 8 repeated the way I’m handling it in my master’s: OOR values left out of the tests, nothing substituted.


Show the code: repeat the screen with OOR values left out

  filter(Visit == "Baseline", tb_diagnosis %in% c("Active TB", "Control")) |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(
    pct_oor = mean(below | above) * 100,
    # value is NA wherever the assay reported an OOR code, so these use detected values only
    ratio_out = exp(mean(log(value[tb_diagnosis == "Active TB"]), na.rm = TRUE) -
                    mean(log(value[tb_diagnosis == "Control"]), na.rm = TRUE)),
    p_out = wilcox.test(value ~ tb_diagnosis, exact = FALSE)$p.value,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(q_out = p.adjust(p_out, method = "BH"))

screen |>
  select(cytokine, ratio, p, q_bh) |>
  inner_join(screen_left_out, by = "cytokine") |>
  filter(pct_oor > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_oor)) |>
  transmute(cytokine,
            pct_oor = round(pct_oor, 1),
            effect  = if_else(cytokine %in% built_in, "Yes", "No"),
            ratio   = round(ratio, 2), ratio_out = round(ratio_out, 2),
            across(c(p, p_out, q_bh, q_out), \(x) sapply(x, format.pval, digits = 2, eps = 1e-16))) |>

With the OOR values left out, Benjamini-Hochberg finds 6 significant cytokines instead of 7, and three results change:

IL-10 is missed. Its real effect is no longer significant (q = 0.27, against 0.002 with the values kept).
IL-6’s ratio shrinks from 1.92 to 1.54. It’s still significant, but the effect looks smaller than the one built into the simulation, because the ratio now compares only the samples where IL-6 was detected.
IL-13 moves towards a false positive. It has no effect in the simulation, but its uncorrected p-value falls from 0.32 to 0.016. Correction keeps it out (q = 0.06), only just.

For cytokines with only a few percent OOR, such as IL-2 and IL-17A, the two approaches barely differ. The gap grows with the share of OOR values. Whichever approach you choose, say which one in the methods, and how many values it affected.

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
text:
6. Remember that cytokines move together
The 27 tests aren’t independent. Cytokines measured in the same samples are often correlated, and this simulation includes groups of cytokines that rise and fall together (Figure 4):


Show the code: correlation heatmap
wide <- plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline") |>
  select(Pt_ID, cytokine, conc) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cytokine, values_from = conc)

rho <- cor(wide[cytokines], method = "spearman")
cluster_order <- cytokines[hclust(as.dist(1 - rho))$order]

as_tibble(rho, rownames = "a") |>
  pivot_longer(-a, names_to = "b", values_to = "rho") |>
  mutate(a = factor(a, levels = cluster_order), b = factor(b, levels = cluster_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(a, b, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = orange, mid = "white", high = teal, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Spearman's\nrho") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5))








Figure 4: Spearman correlations between baseline cytokine concentrations (simulated data).





The heatmap uses Spearman’s correlation, which works on ranks, so the values don’t need to be logged or z-scored first: either step would leave every rank, and so the heatmap, unchanged. Those steps matter for a different kind of heatmap, one showing the concentrations themselves (samples by cytokines). There, each cytokine is logged and then z-scored so that cytokines measured in tens and in thousands of pg/ml share one colour scale. Z-scoring only rescales the values; it doesn’t make them any more normal.
Two practical consequences:

Seven significant cytokines aren’t seven independent discoveries. IP-10 and IFN-y correlate (ρ ≈ 0.44 here), so finding both is partly finding the same thing twice. Describe them as a pattern.
Correlated outcomes suit methods that look at all the cytokines together, such as principal component analysis, rather than only one test at a time. My R and Python workflow project shows PCA on a much larger panel.

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
section: 7. Report how big, not just how significant
text:
7. Report how big, not just how significant
A table of stars says nothing about size. For each cytokine, report the ratio between groups (from the log scale) with its confidence interval, alongside the corrected p-value. A volcano plot shows both at once for the whole panel (Figure 5):


Show the code: volcano plot
screen |>
  mutate(significant = q_bh < 0.05,
         q_plot = pmax(q_bh, 1e-16)) |>   # p-values stored as 0 are drawn at 1e-16
  ggplot(aes(log2(ratio), -log10(q_plot), colour = significant)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(data = \(d) filter(d, significant), aes(label = cytokine),
                  size = 3.3, min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.4,
                  seed = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey60", `TRUE` = orange), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "log2 ratio, active TB vs controls", y = "-log10(BH-corrected p)")








Figure 5: Active TB compared with controls at baseline: ratio of geometric means (x, log2 scale) against Benjamini-Hochberg corrected significance (y). Labelled cytokines have q < 0.05; IP-10’s q-value is below 1e-16 and is drawn at that level (simulated data).





The confidence interval for each ratio comes from a t-test on the log values, transformed back (Table 11):


Show the code: ratios with confidence intervals
plasma |>
  filter(Visit == "Baseline", tb_diagnosis %in% c("Active TB", "Control"),
         cytokine %in% c("IP-10", "IFN-y", "IL-10", "Eotaxin")) |>
  mutate(tb_diagnosis = factor(tb_diagnosis, levels = c("Active TB", "Control"))) |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(
    test     = list(t.test(log(conc) ~ tb_diagnosis)),
    ratio    = exp(-diff(test[[1]]$estimate)),
    ci_low   = exp(test[[1]]$conf.int[1]),
    ci_high  = exp(test[[1]]$conf.int[2]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  select(-test) |>
  show_table(digits = 2, col.names = c("Cytokine", "Ratio (active TB ÷ controls)",
                                       "95% CI low", "95% CI high"))




Table 11: Ratio of geometric means, active TB vs controls at baseline, with 95% CIs from t-tests on the log values (simulated data).

“IP-10 was 3.4 times higher in active TB than in controls (95% CI 2.8 to 4.2)” tells a reader far more than “IP-10 ***“.
Two more things stand out. Eotaxin’s interval (1.04 to 1.47) excludes 1, so on its own this single test looks convincing; it’s only once you account for the 27 tests that it drops out, as section 5 showed. And IL-10’s ratio uses substituted values for the 22% of these samples below the limit, so it deserves a caveat in any write-up.

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
section: A checklist for your next panel
text:
A checklist for your next panel

Parse the out-of-range codes. Record below and above the limit; don’t let them become missing values.
Think twice before dropping values below the detection limit. Dropping them can hide real differences. To keep them, use rank-based tests, a stated substitution or censored-data methods; analyse detected vs not when most values are below the limit. Whichever you choose, report it.
Log the concentrations, or use rank-based tests. Don’t run t-tests on raw pg/ml values.
Match the test to the design, and use paired tests for repeated visits on the same people.
Correct for the number of cytokines tested, with Benjamini-Hochberg or Bonferroni.
Treat correlated cytokines as patterns, not independent findings.
Report ratios with confidence intervals, not just stars.

title: Choosing the right statistics for cytokine data
text:
About the simulation
So that you can check the results above against the truth, these are the effects built into the simulated data (on the log scale, as multiples of each cytokine’s typical level):

Active TB: higher IP-10, IFN-y, IL-1ra, IL-6, TNF-a, IL-10 and MCP-1, fading at month 3 and further by month 6.
HIV: higher IP-10, IL-10 and TNF-a.
Every other cytokine: no difference between any groups.

The simulation script, scripts/simulate_plasma_cytokines.py, is in the site’s GitHub repository.

NoteWhat you’ll learn




Audit a dataset to find what needs cleaning
Make category spellings consistent with tolower() and case_when()
Spot missing-value codes that are really an answer

Replace impossible measurements without guessing

title: Cleaning data in R
text:
1. Start where Tutorial 1 ended
Tutorial 1 imported the study metadata and found problems with count() and get_dupes(). This tutorial fixes them. Load the packages (install any you’re missing with install.packages()):

library(readr)      # type_convert(), write_csv()
library(readxl)     # read the Excel file
library(dplyr)      # data manipulation
library(stringr)    # work with text
library(lubridate)  # parse dates
library(janitor)    # clean_names(), get_dupes()
library(here)       # file paths from the project root
library(ggplot2)    # plots to spot problems


metadata_path <- here("data", "bal_metadata.xlsx")

Import the metadata the same way as in Tutorial 1:

missing_codes <- c("", "N/A", "ND", ".", "-", "not done")

metadata <- read_excel(metadata_path, sheet = "MetaData", col_types = "text") |>
  type_convert(na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names()

dim(metadata)

[1] 502  29








TipNever edit the raw file



Do all cleaning in code and leave bal_metadata.xlsx untouched. If you change your mind about a decision, or receive an updated file, you rerun the script. Cleaning by hand in Excel can’t be checked, repeated or undone.

title: Cleaning data in R
Cleaning data in R
text:
3. IDs and duplicates
Participant IDs should be SP followed by five digits. str_detect() with a regular expression finds any that aren’t:

metadata |>
  filter(!str_detect(pt_id, "^SP\\d{5}$")) |>
  select(pt_id)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  pt_id  
  <chr>  
1 sp20422


One ID was typed in lower case. Fix the case and remove stray spaces, then deal with the two participants Tutorial 1 found entered twice. Their two rows are identical in every column, so distinct() safely drops the copies:

metadata_clean <- metadata |>
  mutate(pt_id = toupper(str_trim(pt_id))) |>
  distinct()

nrow(metadata_clean)

[1] 500

n_distinct(metadata_clean$pt_id)

[1] 500


500 rows and 500 IDs: one row per participant.






Warning



distinct() only removes rows that match in every column. If two rows share an ID but differ somewhere (a different age, say), they’re not copies, and you need to find out which one is right before you drop either.

title: Cleaning data in R
text:
4. Consistent spellings

Two-value columns
Most spelling problems are differences in capitals and abbreviations. Lower-case everything first with tolower(), so “FEMALE”, “Female” and “female” all become “female” and you only have to list each answer once. Then use case_when() to say which values mean what. Each line is a condition on the left of ~ and the value to use when it’s true on the right:

clean_sex <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  case_when(
    x %in% c("f", "female") ~ "Female",
    x %in% c("m", "male")   ~ "Male"
  )
}

compare(metadata_clean$sex, clean_sex(metadata_clean$sex))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  before                    after      n
  <chr>                     <chr>  <int>
1 F, female, Female, FEMALE Female   256
2 M, male, Male, MALE       Male     244


Eight spellings become two clean values, one row each. case_when() returns NA for any value that matches none of the conditions. That’s a useful safety net: a spelling you didn’t expect shows up in an NA row of the comparison rather than being quietly lumped in with something else. (You could add a catch-all last line, TRUE ~ "Other", but then unexpected values would hide inside “Other”.)
The yes/no columns (drug_use, vaping, art) and hiv_status follow the same pattern, so one function cleans them all with across():

clean_yes_no <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  case_when(
    x %in% c("y", "yes") ~ "Yes",
    x %in% c("n", "no")  ~ "No"
  )
}

clean_pos_neg <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  case_when(
    x %in% c("pos", "positive") ~ "Positive",
    x %in% c("neg", "negative") ~ "Negative"
  )
}

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(
    sex = clean_sex(sex),
    across(c(drug_use, vaping, art), clean_yes_no),
    hiv_status = clean_pos_neg(hiv_status)
  )

metadata_clean |> count(hiv_status)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  hiv_status     n
  <chr>      <int>
1 Negative     297
2 Positive     203




A few more values
The IGRA result and ethnicity have more than two answers, but the same approach works: list every spelling of each answer.

igra_raw <- tolower(metadata_clean$igra_result)

igra_clean <- case_when(
  igra_raw %in% c("pos", "positive")            ~ "Positive",
  igra_raw %in% c("neg", "negative")            ~ "Negative",
  igra_raw %in% c("indeterminate", "borderline") ~ "Indeterminate"
)

compare(metadata_clean$igra_result, igra_clean)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  before                                   after             n
  <chr>                                    <chr>         <int>
1 Borderline, indeterminate, Indeterminate Indeterminate    68
2 Neg, negative, Negative, NEGATIVE        Negative        166
3 Pos, positive, Positive, POSITIVE        Positive        266

ethnicity_raw <- tolower(metadata_clean$ethnicity)

ethnicity_clean <- case_when(
  ethnicity_raw == "black african"                        ~ "Black African",
  ethnicity_raw %in% c("coloured", "mixed", "mixed race") ~ "Coloured",
  ethnicity_raw == "white"                                ~ "White",
  ethnicity_raw == "asian"                                ~ "Asian"
)

compare(metadata_clean$ethnicity, ethnicity_clean)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  before                                          after             n
  <chr>                                           <chr>         <int>
1 asian, Asian                                    Asian            82
2 black african, Black African, BLACK AFRICAN     Black African   119
3 coloured, Coloured, COLOURED, Mixed, mixed race Coloured        189
4 white, White, WHITE                             White           110

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(igra_result = igra_clean, ethnicity = ethnicity_clean)

Two of these are decisions, so they go in the decision log:

A borderline IGRA is too close to the cut-off to call positive or negative, so it joins Indeterminate: in both cases the test didn’t give a usable answer.
“Mixed” and “mixed race” describe the same group as Coloured, the term used in the South African census, so all three become Coloured.



Columns that need a decision
Some columns can’t be cleaned by fixing capitals alone. You have to decide what the values mean.
Smoking status has ex, Ex-smoker and Former, which clearly mean the same thing, and yes for current smokers. But it also has both never and no. “No” probably means “doesn’t smoke now”, which could include former smokers who answered loosely. Here we treat no as “Never”, and write that decision down (see section 9):

smoking_raw <- tolower(metadata_clean$smoking_status)

smoking <- case_when(
  smoking_raw == "yes"                          ~ "Current",
  smoking_raw %in% c("ex", "ex-smoker", "former") ~ "Former",
  smoking_raw %in% c("never", "no")              ~ "Never"
)

compare(metadata_clean$smoking_status, smoking)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  before                        after       n
  <chr>                         <chr>   <int>
1 yes, Yes, YES                 Current   122
2 ex, Ex, EX, Ex-smoker, Former Former    214
3 never, no, No, NO             Never     164

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(smoking_status = factor(smoking, levels = c("Never", "Former", "Current")))

Drug type needs local knowledge: tik is South African slang for crystal methamphetamine, so tik and crystal meth are the same drug. Only one value changes. The last line, TRUE ~ drug_type, is a condition that is always true, so every value not matched above it keeps its current value. str_to_sentence() then fixes the capitals:

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(
    drug_type = tolower(drug_type),
    drug_type = case_when(
      drug_type == "tik" ~ "crystal meth",
      TRUE               ~ drug_type   # keep every other value
    ),
    drug_type = str_to_sentence(drug_type)
  )

metadata_clean |> count(drug_type)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  drug_type        n
  <chr>        <int>
1 Cannabis        42
2 Crystal meth   105
3 Heroin          21
4 Mandrax         48
5 Multiple        42
6 <NA>           242








TipTRUE ~ or .default



Since dplyr 1.1.0 you can write the catch-all as .default = drug_type instead of TRUE ~ drug_type. Both do the same thing; TRUE ~ also works in older versions, and you’ll see it in most existing code. Use a catch-all only when you mean “leave everything else as it is”, as here. When you’re mapping spellings to categories, leave it out so unexpected values show up as NA.




Ordered categories
Sputum smear grade was recorded in 21 ways, including +2, 2 +, two plus and 0 for negative. Removing spaces first leaves fewer variants to list. The grades have a natural order, so store them as an ordered factor; later analyses can then treat Scanty < 1+ < 2+ < 3+ correctly:

smear_raw <- metadata_clean$smear_grade |>
  tolower() |>
  str_remove_all("\\s")

smear <- case_when(
  smear_raw %in% c("0", "neg", "negative")  ~ "Negative",
  smear_raw %in% c("scant", "scanty")       ~ "Scanty",
  smear_raw %in% c("1+", "+1", "oneplus")   ~ "1+",
  smear_raw %in% c("2+", "+2", "twoplus")   ~ "2+",
  smear_raw %in% c("3+", "+3", "threeplus") ~ "3+"
)

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(smear_grade = factor(smear,
    levels = c("Negative", "Scanty", "1+", "2+", "3+"), ordered = TRUE))

metadata_clean |> count(smear_grade)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  smear_grade     n
  <ord>       <int>
1 Negative      351
2 Scanty         43
3 1+             39
4 2+             45
5 3+             22




Free-text categories
Chest X-ray findings are closer to free text. case_when() can test keywords with str_detect() as well as exact values. It checks the conditions from top to bottom and uses the first one that’s true, so the order matters, and so does choosing the right keyword:

cxr_original <- metadata_clean$cxr_finding
cxr <- tolower(cxr_original)

# A tempting shortcut: anything containing "normal" is normal
shortcut <- case_when(
  str_detect(cxr, "normal") ~ "Normal",
  TRUE                      ~ "Abnormal"
)

compare(cxr_original, shortcut) |>
  filter(after == "Normal")

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  before                                                                      after      n
  <chr>                                                                       <chr>  <int>
1 Abnormal - other, No abnormality, normal, Normal, NORMAL, Other abnormality Normal   252


The shortcut goes wrong twice. “abnormal - other” and “other abnormality” both contain the word “normal”, so abnormal X-rays are called normal. And “NAD” (no abnormality detected) doesn’t contain it, so normal X-rays are called abnormal. Match normal findings exactly, and use keywords only for the abnormal ones:

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(cxr_finding = case_when(
    cxr %in% c("normal", "nad", "no abnormality") ~ "Normal",
    str_detect(cxr, "cavit")                      ~ "Cavitation",
    str_detect(cxr, "infiltrate|consolidation")   ~ "Infiltrate/consolidation",
    cxr == "pleural effusion"                     ~ "Pleural effusion",
    cxr == "fibrosis"                             ~ "Fibrosis",
    str_detect(cxr, "other")                      ~ "Other abnormality"
  ))

compare(cxr_original, metadata_clean$cxr_finding)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  before                                                                         after                        n
  <chr>                                                                          <chr>                    <int>
1 cavitary, Cavitary, cavitation, Cavitation, Cavity noted                       Cavitation                  66
2 Fibrosis                                                                       Fibrosis                     9
3 consolidation, Consolidation, infiltrate, Infiltrate, Infiltrate/Consolidation Infiltrate/consolidation    78
4 NAD, No abnormality, normal, Normal, NORMAL                                    Normal                     301
5 Abnormal - other, Other, Other abnormality                                     Other abnormality           33
6 Pleural effusion                                                               Pleural effusion            13


NAD is the clinical abbreviation for “no abnormality detected”. Fourteen spellings now fall into six categories, and there’s no NA row.


Many variants: use a lookup table
referral_source has 49 versions of the referring clinic’s name, including full names, abbreviations (BV CHC, KDH) and a misspelling (Mitchells Plein). A case_when() with 49 values would work, but a lookup table is easier to read and to update. First, let rules remove the differences that don’t matter, so there are fewer variants to look up:

referral_key <- metadata_clean$referral_source |>
  tolower() |>
  str_remove_all("'") |>
  str_remove(" (chc|community health( centre)?|hosp(ital)?|district hospital|dhc)$")

n_distinct(referral_key)

[1] 20


Then write one row per remaining variant, and join:

referral_lookup <- tribble(
  ~referral_key,     ~referral_site,
  "bellville",       "Bellville CHC",
  "bv",              "Bellville CHC",
  "claremont",       "Claremont CHC",
  "cchc",            "Claremont CHC",
  "delft",           "Delft CHC",
  "dchc",            "Delft CHC",
  "eerste river",    "Eerste River Hospital",
  "erh",             "Eerste River Hospital",
  "elsies river",    "Elsies River CHC",
  "erchc",           "Elsies River CHC",
  "khayelitsha",     "Khayelitsha District Hospital",
  "kdh",             "Khayelitsha District Hospital",
  "mitchells plain", "Mitchells Plain District Hospital",
  "mitchells plein", "Mitchells Plain District Hospital",
  "mp",              "Mitchells Plain District Hospital",
  "ottery",          "Ottery CHC",
  "retreat",         "Retreat CHC",
  "somerset",        "Somerset Hospital",
  "woodstock",       "Woodstock CHC",
  "ws",              "Woodstock CHC"
)

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(referral_key = referral_key) |>
  left_join(referral_lookup, by = "referral_key") |>
  select(-referral_key, -referral_source)

metadata_clean |> count(referral_site)

# A tibble: 11 × 2
   referral_site                         n
   <chr>                             <int>
 1 Bellville CHC                        47
 2 Claremont CHC                        41
 3 Delft CHC                            54

49 spellings became 11 clinics, and no rows were left without a site. If a new spelling appears in an updated file, it comes through the join as NA, so the check filter(is.na(referral_site)) finds it and you add one row to the lookup table.






Note



ERCHC could stand for Elsies River CHC or Eerste River CHC. No Eerste River CHC appears anywhere else in the data (only the hospital), so we map it to Elsies River CHC. That’s an assumption, so it goes in the decision log, and ideally you’d confirm it with whoever entered the data.

title: Cleaning data in R
text:
5. When “missing” is really a category
Tutorial 1 treated N/A and ND as missing. For most columns that’s right, but not for the rifampicin-resistance result (GeneXpert_RIF). In the Excel file it holds Sensitive, Resistant and Indeterminate, plus three codes: N/A, Not applicable and ND (not done). They look like three different things. Read the original text again and check where they occur:

rif_original <- read_excel(metadata_path, sheet = "MetaData", col_types = "text") |>
  transmute(pt_id = toupper(Pt_ID), mtb_result = tolower(GeneXpert_Res), rif = GeneXpert_RIF) |>
  distinct()

rif_original |>
  filter(rif %in% c("N/A", "Not applicable", "ND")) |>
  count(mtb_result)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  mtb_result           n
  <chr>            <int>
1 error               19
2 indeterminate       10
3 invalid             11
4 mtb not detected   212


None of them occurs when TB was detected. GeneXpert only reports rifampicin resistance when it detects M. tuberculosis, so all three codes mean the same thing: there’s no resistance result because there was no TB to test. That’s a real answer, not missing data. But Tutorial 1’s missing-value codes turned N/A and ND into NA while Not applicable stayed as text, splitting one group into two.
The fix is to derive the RIF result from the rule instead of relying on whichever code was typed: first clean the MTB result, then set the RIF result to “Not applicable” whenever MTB wasn’t detected.
The MTB result also has three labels for a failed test: Error, Invalid and Indeterminate. None of them gives a usable result, and each group is small, so combine them into one “No result” category:

xpert_original <- metadata_clean$gene_xpert_res
xpert_raw <- tolower(xpert_original)

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(
    gene_xpert_res = case_when(
      xpert_raw == "mtb detected"                           ~ "MTB detected",
      xpert_raw == "mtb not detected"                       ~ "MTB not detected",
      xpert_raw %in% c("error", "invalid", "indeterminate") ~ "No result"
    ),
    gene_xpert_rif = case_when(
      gene_xpert_res == "MTB detected" ~ gene_xpert_rif,
      TRUE                             ~ "Not applicable"
    )
  )

compare(xpert_original, metadata_clean$gene_xpert_res)

rif_check <- rif_original |>
  left_join(select(metadata_clean, pt_id, gene_xpert_rif), by = "pt_id")

N/A, ND and Not applicable are now one “Not applicable” group. The “Not applicable” row also takes in some Sensitive and Indeterminate entries: 66 rows recorded “Sensitive” for a sample where no TB was detected, which is impossible, and the rule corrects them. Every participant with MTB detected keeps their resistance result.






Tip



When one column depends on another, derive it from the rule rather than trusting what was typed. Then a data-entry mistake in the dependent column can’t get through.

6. Dates in mixed formats
date_seen was entered as text in several formats:

metadata_clean |>
  filter(!str_detect(date_seen, "^\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{4}$")) |>
  distinct(date_seen) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 1
  date_seen

1 09-09-2020  
2 17-07-2017  
3 12-07-2017  
4 09-02-2019

dmy() from lubridate reads day-month-year dates whatever the separator, two-digit years and month names included. Use it, then look at what failed:

date_seen <- dmy(metadata_clean$date_seen, quiet = TRUE)

metadata_clean$date_seen[is.na(date_seen)]

[1] "08/20/2017" "12/26/2016" "06/26/2020" "07/28/2020" "10/17/2018" "08/16/2018" "03/19/2016"
[8] "08/21/2020"


These 8 dates fail because they’re in American month/day/year order: there’s no 20th month. Read the failures with mdy(), and use coalesce() to fill each gap from the second attempt:

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(
    date_seen      = coalesce(dmy(date_seen, quiet = TRUE), mdy(date_seen, quiet = TRUE)),
    art_start_date = coalesce(dmy(art_start_date, quiet = TRUE), mdy(art_start_date, quiet = TRUE))
  )

range(metadata_clean$date_seen)

[1] "2016-01-04" "2020-12-08"

sum(is.na(metadata_clean$date_seen))

[1] 0


All dates parse, and they fall within the study period (2016–2020).






WarningSome date errors can’t be detected



A US-format date such as 03/04/2018 is a valid day-month-year date too (3 April instead of 4 March), so dmy() reads it without complaint. Only dates with a day above 12 give themselves away. The real fix is upstream: ask for dates in one unambiguous format such as 2018-03-04 when the data is collected.

title: Cleaning data in R
text:
7. Impossible measurements
summary() quickly shows values that can’t be right:

metadata_clean |>
  select(age, height_1_cm, height_2_cm, weight_1_kg, weight_2_kg) |>
  summary()

                 NAs    :17       NAs    :14      NAs    :18       NAs    :22      


Heights of −170 cm and 1,863 cm, and weights of 999 kg. Each participant was measured twice, so plotting the two measurements against each other shows the problems clearly. Good pairs fall on the diagonal:

ggplot(metadata_clean, aes(weight_1_kg, weight_2_kg)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Weight, first measurement (kg)", y = "Weight, second measurement (kg)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: First and second weight measurements. Values far from the diagonal are entry errors: negative signs, missing decimal points, and 999 or 500 used as codes.





The errors are recognisable: 999 and 500 used as “missing” codes, a minus sign typed by mistake (-72.5), and a missing decimal point (814 for 81.4). It’s tempting to repair them (divide by 10, drop the minus sign), but each repair is a guess. Because every participant has a second measurement, there’s no need to guess:

Set any value outside a plausible range to NA.
Use the mean of the remaining measurements. If one is missing, use the other.


# Keep values inside the range; anything else becomes NA
plausible <- function(x, lower, upper) {
  case_when(
    between(x, lower, upper) ~ x,
    TRUE                     ~ NA
  )
}

# The mean of two values; if one is missing, the other one
mean_of_two <- function(a, b) (coalesce(a, b) + coalesce(b, a)) / 2

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  mutate(
    across(starts_with("height"), \(x) plausible(x, 100, 220)),
    across(starts_with("weight"), \(x) plausible(x, 25, 250)),
    height_cm = mean_of_two(height_1_cm, height_2_cm),
    weight_kg = mean_of_two(weight_1_kg, weight_2_kg),
    bmi       = weight_kg / (height_cm / 100)^2
  ) |>
  select(-matches("_[12]_(cm|kg)$"))

  select(height_cm, weight_kg, bmi) |>
  summary()

section: 8. Duplicate columns and rows to review

8. Duplicate columns and rows to review
Some problems only appear when you compare columns. study_group looks like tb_diagnosis:

metadata_clean |> count(study_group == tb_diagnosis)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  `study_group == tb_diagnosis`     n
  <lgl>                         <int>
1 TRUE                            500


They’re identical on every row, so drop study_group; keeping two copies invites them to drift apart later.
The very low BMIs from section 7 could be real or a recording error, and the data alone can’t tell you which. Don’t guess: flag the rows and send the list to the study team:

metadata_clean <- metadata_clean |>
  select(-study_group) |>
  mutate(review_bmi = !is.na(bmi) & bmi < 13)

metadata_clean |> count(review_bmi)

# A tibble: 2 × 2

  <lgl>      <int>
1 FALSE        494
2 TRUE           6


Analyses can then include or exclude these rows deliberately, and you can update them when the answers come back.

    sex          = factor(sex)

text:
Try it yourself
Two columns are left for you, using the same patterns:

art_regimen has 10 spellings of what are really two regimens: TLD (tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir) and efavirenz-based ones such as TEE. Use tolower() and case_when() to reduce it to TLD and Efavirenz-based.
vaping_type mixes capitals (pod, Pod). Clean the case. Then decide whether Juul, a brand of pod device, should be its own category or grouped with Pod, and add the decision to your log.

title: Cleaning data in R
text:
Common pitfalls








Problem
Symptom
Fix




Cleaning in Excel
Changes can’t be checked or repeated
Leave the raw file alone; clean in code


Unlisted spellings
New NA values after recoding
compare() before and after; leave out a TRUE ~ catch-all so case_when() returns NA for anything unlisted


Keyword matches too much
“Abnormal” counted as “normal”
Match exact values first, keywords second


Missing codes that are really an answer
One group split into NA and “Not applicable”
Check where the codes occur; derive values from the rule where you can


Capitals
“Female”, “FEMALE” and “female” listed separately
tolower() before matching


Mixed date formats
dmy() returns NA for some dates
Check the failures; coalesce() a second format


Guessing at errors
814 “fixed” to 81.4
Use a repeat measurement, or set to NA


Silent fixes to conflicting data
Nobody knows a value was changed
Flag rows for review instead


Vector named like a column
mutate(sex = sex) silently keeps the old column
Give cleaned vectors their own names (sex_clean)


Alphabetical categories
Tables start with “Active TB”
Set factor levels in a sensible order

title: Importing data into RStudio with R
text:
1. Set up an RStudio Project
Start every analysis in an RStudio Project (File → New Project). A project sets the working directory to the project folder, so file paths are the same on every computer that opens it.
A simple layout:
my-analysis/
├── my-analysis.Rproj
├── data/
│   ├── bal_metadata.xlsx
│   ├── bal_cell_counts.xlsx
│   └── bal_baseline.csv
└── analysis.qmd
Put the three downloaded files in data/, then load the packages used in this tutorial (install any you’re missing with install.packages()):

library(readr)    # fast, consistent CSV reading
library(readxl)   # Excel files (.xls and .xlsx)
library(dplyr)    # data manipulation
library(purrr)    # repeat a step over many sheets
library(janitor)  # tidy column names, find duplicates
library(here)     # build file paths from the project root
library(ggplot2)  # a quick plot to check the data

here() builds a path starting from the project root, wherever your script lives:

# In your own project:
metadata_path <- here("data", "bal_metadata.xlsx")







Tip



Avoid setwd("C:/Users/me/Desktop/..."). A hard-coded path only works on your own computer, and breaks as soon as you move the folder or share it.

Two things stand out:

The column names contain brackets and slashes (Height_1(cm), IGRA_Value(IU/ml)), so you’d have to wrap them in backticks every time you use them.
Height, weight and IGRA value should be numbers, but they were read as text (<chr>).

Why are they text? Look at the values that aren’t numbers:

metadata_raw |>
  filter(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(`Height_1(cm)`))),
         !is.na(`Height_1(cm)`)) |>
  count(`Height_1(cm)`, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  `Height_1(cm)`     n
  <chr>          <int>
1 -                  4
2 .                  4
3 N/A                3
4 ND                 3
5 not done           3


The people who entered the data recorded “missing” in five different ways. One text value is enough to make the whole column text. Tell read_excel() which codes mean missing with the na argument, and use clean_names() to fix the column names:

missing_codes <- c("", "N/A", "ND", ".", "-", "not done")

read_excel(metadata_path, sheet = "MetaData", na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names() |>
  select(pt_id, age, height_1_cm, weight_1_kg, igra_value_iu_ml) |>
  glimpse()

Rows: 502
Columns: 5
$ pt_id            <chr> "SP34696", "SP22845", "SP31186", "SP39161", "SP06180"…
$ age              <dbl> 53, 30, 15, 50, 30, 35, 54, 38, 20, 43, 44, 27, 24, 4…
$ height_1_cm      <chr> "182.6", "160.3", "143.9", "165.8", "173.8", "172", "…

The reliable fix is to read the sheet as text, then let readr::type_convert() guess each column’s type from its contents, treating the missing-value codes as NA:

metadata <- read_excel(metadata_path, sheet = "MetaData", col_types = "text") |>
  type_convert(na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names()

metadata |>
  select(pt_id, age, height_1_cm, weight_1_kg, igra_value_iu_ml) |>

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
NoteAt a glance




What: a modular Nextflow DSL2 pipeline that turns raw paired-end whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reads into a joint-called, quality-filtered set of variants
Tools: Nextflow, BWA-MEM, SAMtools and GATK4, with FastQC and MultiQC for read quality control
Where: built for my BSc Honours project at Stellenbosch University (2024) and run on the Centre for High Performance Computing (CHPC) cluster
Scope of this page: how the pipeline is designed and how it works. It contains no study data and no results.

View the code on GitHub

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
Why I built it
My honours project compared variant calls made against the standard human reference genome, GRCh38 (Schneider et al., 2017), with calls made against a population-specific reference genome.
That comparison set three requirements:

Reproducible: every sample goes through exactly the same steps, with the same tools and settings.
Reference-agnostic: the same pipeline runs against either reference with a single switch, keeping the outputs apart.
HPC-friendly: whole genomes produce very large intermediate files, so the pipeline has to fit a shared cluster’s storage, memory and wall-time limits.

Nextflow (Di Tommaso et al., 2017) fits all three: each step is an isolated process, runs are resumable, and the same code can run on a laptop or a PBS cluster.

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
How it works






flowchart LR
    A[Paired-end<br/>FASTQ] --> B[Align<br/>BWA-MEM]
    B --> C[SAM → BAM<br/>sort, index<br/>SAMtools]
    C --> D[Base quality<br/>recalibration<br/>GATK BQSR]
    D --> E[Per-sample<br/>GVCF<br/>HaplotypeCaller]
    E --> F[Joint genotyping<br/>GenomicsDBImport<br/>GenotypeGVCFs]
    F --> G[Variant filtering<br/>VQSR<br/>SNPs + indels]
    G --> H[Filtered<br/>cohort VCF]






Read quality was checked with FastQC (Andrews, 2010) and summarised across samples with MultiQC (Ewels et al., 2016) before reads entered the pipeline. The pipeline then follows GATK’s best-practice workflow for germline short variants (Van der Auwera and O’Connor, 2020):








Step
Tool (version)
What it does




Align
BWA-MEM 0.7.7 (Li and Durbin, 2009; Li, 2013)
Maps each sample’s read pairs to the chosen reference, adding a read group (sample, library, MGI platform) that GATK needs downstream


Convert, sort, index
SAMtools 1.9 (Danecek et al., 2021)
Converts the text SAM output to compressed BAM, sorts reads by position and indexes them


Recalibrate base qualities
GATK 4.6 BaseRecalibrator and ApplyBQSR (McKenna et al., 2010; DePristo et al., 2011)
Corrects systematic errors in the sequencer’s base quality scores, using dbSNP (Sherry, Ward and Sirotkin, 1999) as known variant sites


Call variants per sample
GATK 4.6 HaplotypeCaller, GVCF mode (Poplin et al., 2017)
Calls variants by local re-assembly and records every position, so samples can be genotyped together later


Joint genotyping
GATK 4.6 GenomicsDBImport and GenotypeGVCFs (Poplin et al., 2017)
Combines all samples’ GVCFs, chromosome by chromosome (1–22, X, Y), and genotypes them as one cohort


Filter variants
GATK 4.2.6 VariantRecalibrator and ApplyVQSR (DePristo et al., 2011)
Learns what true variants look like from trusted resources and filters the rest at 99% truth sensitivity, with separate models for SNPs and indels



The variant filtering step trains on well-established resources: HapMap 3.3 (International HapMap 3 Consortium, 2010) and the 1000 Genomes Omni 2.5 genotypes (The 1000 Genomes Project Consortium, 2015) for SNPs, the Mills and 1000 Genomes gold-standard indels (Mills et al., 2011) for indels, and dbSNP (Sherry, Ward and Sirotkin, 1999) as known sites. The filtered SNPs and indels are then merged into a single indexed cohort VCF.

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
Engineering details

One module per step
Each step is a separate DSL2 module (modules/local/<step>/main.nf), and the main workflow only wires them together. That keeps each step small, testable and easy to swap out:


script.nf (excerpt)

workflow {
    aligned_sams = ALIGN(samples_ch, reference_ch)
    aligned_bams = SAM_TO_BAM(aligned_sams)
    sorted_bams  = SORT_BAM(aligned_bams)
    indexed_bams = INDEX_BAM(sorted_bams.sorted_bam)

    bqsr_bams = BQSR(indexed_bams, reference_ch, reference_index_ch,
                     reference_dict_ch, dbsnp_ch, dbsnp_index_ch)

    gvcfs = HAPLOTYPECALLER(bqsr_bams, reference_ch,
                            reference_index_ch, reference_dict_ch)
    // ... joint genotyping and variant filtering
}



One switch for the reference genome
A single parameter chooses the reference. Outputs are named and stored separately per reference, so a GRCh38 run and a population-reference run never overwrite each other:


modules/local/haplotypecaller/main.nf (excerpt)

publishDir "${params.outdir}/haplotypecaller/${params.use_sac_ref ? 'sac' : 'grch38'}",
           mode: 'symlink'



Dry runs without data
Every module has a stub: block that creates empty placeholder outputs. Running nextflow run script.nf -stub checks that all the channels connect correctly in seconds, without real data and without using cluster time:


modules/local/bqsr/main.nf (excerpt)

stub:
"""
touch ${sampleId}.recal.bam
touch ${sampleId}.recal.bai
"""



Fitting a shared cluster

Storage: an aligned whole genome in SAM format can be tens of gigabytes. Intermediate outputs are published as symbolic links (mode: 'symlink') rather than copies, and only the final filtered VCF is copied.
Resources: memory and CPUs are set per process, so heavy steps such as alignment get what they need without over-allocating light ones.
Software: each process loads its own pinned tool version through the cluster’s environment modules.



nextflow.config (excerpt, cluster details replaced)

process {
    queue          = 'normal'
    clusterOptions = '-P <project-code>'

    withName: 'ALIGN' {
        beforeScript = 'module load BWA/0.7.7'
        memory = '38 GB'
    }
    withName: 'HAPLOTYPECALLER' {
        beforeScript = 'module load gatk/4.6.0.0'
        memory = '8 GB'
        cpus   = 5
    }
}



Joint calling that scales
Calling each sample to a GVCF first, then genotyping the cohort together, means that adding samples later only needs the new samples to be called. It also improves genotype accuracy at sites with low coverage in some samples (Poplin et al., 2017).

title: A Nextflow Pipeline for Whole-Genome Variant Calling
text:
What I’d do differently
Looking back, these are the changes I would make:

Mark duplicates before recalibration. GATK’s best practices include MarkDuplicates between alignment and BQSR (Van der Auwera and O’Connor, 2020); the pipeline goes straight from sorting to BQSR.
Stream instead of writing SAM files. Piping bwa mem directly into samtools sort would skip the large intermediate SAM files entirely.
Make quality control part of the pipeline. FastQC and MultiQC were configured but run separately; wiring them in would make each run fully self-contained.
Use containers and profiles. Docker or Singularity containers and Nextflow configuration profiles, instead of cluster-specific modules and paths, would let the pipeline run unchanged on any system.
Use one GATK version throughout. Variant filtering ran on GATK 4.2.6 while the other GATK steps used 4.6.
Compare references against a truth set. Counting shared and unique variants between two references shows that the call sets differ, but not which is more accurate: a reference that already contains a population’s common alleles will report fewer variants at those sites by design. A fair comparison needs a truth set, such as array genotypes for the same samples.

Analytical and Clinical Objective
The primary objective of this project is to build and evaluate a 3-class machine learning classifier (Active TB vs. Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) vs. Uninfected) using the multiplex cytokine panel. Model performance will be bench-marked directly against the World Health Organization (WHO) Target Product Profile (TPP) for a TB triage test, which requires a minimum acceptable performance threshold of \(≥90%\) sensitivity and \(≥70\%\) specificity.

title: Compartmental TB Diagnostics: A Simulated BAL Cytokine Cohort
text:
Library import
This project implements a multilingual data science workflow, utilising R for data engineering and statistical analysis, and Python for predictive modelling. Data ingestion, programmatic cleaning, and parsing are executed using the R tidyverse core ecosystem, specifically dplyr (Wickham et al., 2026), tidyr (Wickham, Vaughan and Girlich, 2026), stringr (Wickham, 2025), and janitor (Firke, 2024). Descriptive clinical tables and baseline group statistics are compiled using the R packages gtsummary (Sjoberg et al., 2021) and broom (Robinson et al., n.d.), while exploratory data visualisation and dimensional reduction are conducted via ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016) and factoextra (Kassambara and Mundt, 2026).
If the analytical scope expands to predictive modelling, the workflow transitions to Python via the reticulate (Ushey, Allaire and Tang, 2025) interface. This pipeline leverages Python’s machine learning libraries, including scikit-learn for cross-validation and evaluation metrics, xgboost for gradient-boosted decision tree architecture, and shap for model feature attribution.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Why I built this
Most of my work so far has been in clinical genomics and tuberculosis research. I wanted a project that showed the same skills (messy data, careful pipelines, honest modelling) applied to a business problem, and credit risk is one of the most common uses of data science in South African banking and insurance.
The lender in this project needs to answer three questions:

Which applicants are likely to default? A model that ranks new applicants by risk at the point of application.
Where is the portfolio risk concentrated? Default rates by province, channel and time.
Which marketing campaigns are worth the money? Cost per application and cost per approved loan.

text:
Architecture






flowchart LR
    A[Source files] --> B[Bronze<br/>raw + lineage]
    B --> C[Silver<br/>cleaned and validated]
    C --> D[Gold<br/>model-ready tables]
    D --> E[Models<br/>MLflow]
    D --> F[Dashboard and<br/>risk report]

Layer
What happens




Bronze
Source files loaded as-is, with lineage columns recording the source file, sheet and ingestion time


Silver
IDs standardised, money, numbers and dates parsed, categories mapped, out-of-range values nulled, duplicates removed, quality checks enforced


Gold
One row per loan with application-time features and a default label, plus campaign attribution and efficiency tables


Model

One notebook, 00_run_all, runs every stage in order and prints a summary of the gold table and the latest model results.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Cleaning messy data
The source data has the kinds of problems real lending data has. Rather than fixing them ad hoc, I wrote shared functions in src/cleaning.py that every notebook uses.







Problem in the source
How the pipeline handles it




IDs written as c00042, C 0042, 42
Standardised to C00042


Money as R 7350, R7,350, 7350.00
Currency symbols, spaces and commas stripped


Dates in seven formats, some with two-digit years
Each format tried in turn; dates outside a valid range rejected


Null markers such as N/A, ND, unknown, -
Recognised by one shared pattern and treated as missing


Free-text categories (gau, Gauteng, GAUTENG)
Mapped to standard values; ambiguous ones (Nor) reported and left blank rather than guessed


Campaigns with swapped dates or negative spend
Corrected and flagged



For example, a single function handles every money format:
def parse_money(df, c):
    """'R 7350', 'R7,350', '7350.00' -> 7350.0"""
    t = F.regexp_replace(F.trim(F.col(c)), r"[Rr,\s]", "")
    return df.withColumn(
        c,
        F.when(F.col(c).rlike(NULL_TOKENS), F.lit(None).cast("double"))
         .otherwise(t.try_cast("double")),
    )
Every silver table must also pass checks before it is written: unique keys, no unparsed dates, and no orphaned records (for example, repayments for a loan that does not exist). If a check fails, the pipeline stops, so bad data never reaches the gold layer.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Building a leakage-free loan table
The gold layer is where most of the modelling decisions live. Three of them matter most.
1. Only use what was known at application time. For example, the number of previous applications counts only those made before the current one:
w = (Window.partitionBy("customer_id")
     .orderBy("application_date", "application_id")
     .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, -1))
apps = apps.withColumn("n_prior_applications", F.count("*").over(w))
2. A clear definition of default. A loan counts as defaulted if it reaches 90+ days past due within its first 6 instalments, or within the full term for shorter loans.
3. Only label loans that have been watched long enough. A loan that has defaulted after three months is easy to label, but a loan that is three months old and still paying might default next month. Labelling it “no default” too early would make recent loans look safer than they are. So loans that have not been observed for the full window get no label:
defaulted = F.col("max_dpd") >= 90
matured = F.col("n_observed") >= window_len

g = (g.withColumn("matured", F.coalesce(matured, F.lit(False)))
      .withColumn("default_flag", F.when(F.col("matured"), defaulted.cast("int"))))
This leaves 6,276 matured loans with a 19.7% default rate for modelling, out of 9,564 in total.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
Modelling
I split the data by time: the model trains on the oldest 80% of loans and is tested on the newest 20%. That is how a lender would actually use it, trained on past customers and applied to future ones. A random split would let the model learn from loans that came after the ones it is tested on.
I compared two models inside the same scikit-learn pipeline (median imputation, scaling and one-hot encoding), with every run logged to MLflow:



Model
Test AUC
Test Gini




Logistic regression
0.668
0.336


Gradient boosting
0.626
0.253



Logistic regression won. With around 5,000 training loans, gradient boosting overfits slightly, while the simpler model generalises better to new loans. Lenders also tend to prefer logistic regression, because each feature’s effect can be explained to regulators and credit committees.
Features used: loan terms (principal, term, interest rate), affordability (income, debt-to-income, loan-to-income), credit history (bureau score, no-bureau-hit flag, prior applications), applicant details (age, employment duration, employer type, province) and channel type.






TipA deliberate exclusion



Sex is in the data but not in the model. South Africa’s National Credit Act prohibits unfair discrimination in credit decisions, and a production scorecard would not use it.

The dashboard is built in Databricks AI/BI on the gold tables and gives a credit manager a one-page view of the portfolio.

title: Credit Risk Pipeline on Databricks
text:
What I learned

Most of the work is in the data, not the model. Cleaning six messy tables and getting the label right took far longer than training, and mattered more for the result.
Data leakage hides in ordinary-looking choices. Using a random split, or labelling recent loans as non-defaulters, would both have produced a better-looking score that would not hold up in practice.
Simpler can be better. The more complex model scored lower on future loans.
Shared, tested functions pay off. Writing the cleaning and quality checks once and reusing them made the pipeline easier to debug and rerun.

text: This analysis evaluates transcriptional variations on Chromosome X (chrX) between male and female individuals to uncover sex-specific dynamics. This study utilises a cohort of 12 paired-end RNA Sequencing (RNAseq) samples obtained from distinct geographical populations. Methods

Data Processing

Differential Expression
Downstream Differential Expression (DE) modelling was performed at the gene level using the Ballgown R package. To isolate sexual differences, phenotypic sex was treated as the primary covariate. Population origin was strictly embedded as a confounding adjustment variable to account for ancestry-driven batch effects. Statistical significance was controlled using False Discovery Rate (FDR) threshold of \(q-value < 0.05\).

Results

Transcript Filtering
An initial set of 2,343 transcripts was extracted from the StringTie quantification step. To eliminate uninformative background noise and improve statistical power, transcripts with low variance across samples were pruned. Applying a filtration cutoff threshold of \(rowVar > 1\) successfully yielded 1,095 high-confidence transcripts retained for exploratory and differential expression processing.


Exploratory Variance Analysis
To understand global relationship structures within the filtered datasets, a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was calculated on transcript-level Fragments Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads (FPKM) expression data.
As plotted in Figure 1, the first two principal components explained 27.1% of total variance (PC1: 14.4%, PC2: 12.7%). The distribution patterns reveal a modest separation based on biological sex along the axis trajectories. Concurrently, clear macro-clusters demonstrate underlying population structure, showing distinct spatial partitioning between European (GBR) and African (YRI) cohorts. This population grouping confirms the necessity of utilising nested model adjustments within the F-test framework to avoid ancestry-driven false-positive discoveries.

TSIX (MSTRG.331): Displays an aligned female bias with an intermediate fold change metric of 0.01181 (\(q = 1.6 \times 10^{-6}\)).
KDM6A (MSTRG.233): Reaches significant separation parameters with an adjusted fold change value of 0.57437 (\(q = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\)).



Gene Abundance Quantification
To validate individual candidate patterns, expression profiles were plotted using log2 (FPKM + 1) metrics. The resulting boxplots (Figure 3) illustrate clear group distributions:

XIST and TSIX Expression: Both features exhibit definitive binary regulation profiles. Abundance levels are highly elevated in females (with median log2 values resting between 6.0 and 9.0) but drop down to zero baseline noise across all male samples. This is consistent with their known roles: XIST drives female-specific X-Chromosome Inactivation (XCI), while TSIX acts as its antisense regulator partner.
KDM6A Expression: Unlike the regulatory Ribonucleic acid (RNA), KDM6A is actively transcribed in both sexes. However, female samples present a statistically elevated expression ceiling compared to male profiles. This matches its classification as an XCI-escape gene that regularly maintains dual-dosage activity in female tissue.

title: Differential Expression Analysis of Chromosome X RNA-seq Data
text:
Discussion and Conclusion

Biological Implications of Female-Biased Expression
The differential expression analysis of human Chromosome X transcripts revealed a highly localised regulatory signature. Only three genes - XIST, TSIX, and KDM6A - exhibited statistically significant expression differences between sexes (\(q < 0.05\)). All three candidates demonstrated explicit female-biased abundance. This tight localisation underscores the stringent evolutionary conservation governing sex-chromosome dosage mechanisms in humans.


Mechanistic Synergy of XIST and TSIX
The identification of XIST (MSTRG.332) and TSIX (MSTRG.331) as the most statistically significant differentially expressed features aligns with established models of XCI (Lyon, 1961; Galupa and Heard, 2018). In female mammals, dosage compensation between XX and XY individuals is achieved by transcriptionally silencing one of the two female X chromosomes.

XIST Function: This long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) is transcribed exclusively from the future inactive X chromosome (\(X_i\)). It physically coats the chromosome in cis, recruiting repressive chromatin-modifying complexes to initiate heterochromatin silencing.
TSIX Function: Operating as an antisense lncRNA partner, TSIX is transcribed from the opposite strand (Lee and Lu, 1999) and overlaps the XIST locus. It acts as a negative regulator of XIST. Prior to inactivation, TSIX expression on the future active X chromosome (\(X_a\)) represses XIST accumulation, preserving transcription.

The binary expression profiles captured in the FPKM boxplots (Figure 3) — where both lncRNAs show near-zero baseline expression across all male samples — reflect this strict functional biology. Because males possess only a single, active X chromosome, the XIST/TSIX inactivation locus is never activated.


Dosage Escape by KDM6A
The significant female bias observed in KDM6A (MSTRG.233) highlights a distinct biological phenomenon: XCI escape. KDM6A encodes a histone demethylase responsible for removing repressive H3K27me3 marks, thereby promoting transcriptionally active chromatin states.
Unlike XIST and TSIX, KDM6A maintains active transcription in male individuals. However, its elevated expression in females confirms that it escapes complete epigenetic silencing (Balaton, Cotton and Brown, 2015) on the inactive X chromosome. Because KDM6A is transcribed from both the active and inactive X chromosomes in females, it avoids single-dosage constraint, resulting in a higher steady-state messenger RNA (mRNA) abundance relative to males. This dual-dosage profile may contribute to sex-specific differences in immune responses and oncogenic susceptibility, as KDM6A plays a key role in chromatin remodeling.


Conclusion
By controlling for confounding population structures via Ballgown’s nested F-test framework, this study isolated true sex-linked transcriptional signals from geographic background noise. The identification of XIST, TSIX, and KDM6A validates the RNAseq processing pipeline, as these targets represent the canonical core of human X-chromosome regulation. The clear separation of population cohorts in the exploratory PCA highlights the necessity of accounting for genetic ancestry in multi-population expression studies to prevent false-positive discoveries.

TipLooking back (November 2026)



This was one of my first portfolio analyses, written in February 2026. If I did it again, I would calculate the key takeaways directly from the data rather than typing them in, and use Welch’s t-test, which doesn’t assume the two groups have equal variances. I would also fit a logistic regression so that age, sex and ventilation are considered together: ventilated patients were probably sicker to begin with, so comparing them directly overstates ventilation’s link with mortality. With 103 patients from one hospital, I would frame the findings more cautiously too. My credit risk pipeline shows how my approach has changed since.

title: COVID-19 Blood Counts and Patient Outcomes
text:
Introduction:
Coronavirus Disease 2019 (Covid-19) is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which emerged as a global pandemic in early 2020. It primarily spreads through respiratory particles and has impacted global health, economics and societies worldwide.

Project Context and Motivation:
This Quarto document serves as an exercise in Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), focusing on a critical public health data-set related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The data, sourced from a collaborative research effort, provides clinical insights into patient outcomes based on complete blood count (CBC) metrics (Rahman et al., 2020) .


Data Source and Collection Methodology:
The data-set was compiled by a team of researchers and medical professionals from Qatar University and Dhaka Medical College Hospital, Bangladesh. Data collection occurred between April 12 and August 31, 2020, at the Dhaka Medical College Hospital, following approval from the local Hospital Ethical Committee. This specific time frame places the data collection during a significant early phase of the pandemic (Rahman et al., 2020).

For alternative R analysis, the comprehensive tidyverse package was loaded (Wickham et al., 2019).

text:
Demographic Distributions:

Patient Age Distribution:








Figure 1: Histogram showing the distribution of patient ages within the dataset.





Figure 1 reveals a multimodal age distribution with peaks around 30-40, 50-60, and 60-70 years, spanning 17, 77 years overall. This middle-aged concentration reflects hospital admission patterns during early pandemic waves. Central tendency centers around 46 years with moderate spread (SD \(\pm\) 16)


Gender Composition:








Figure 2: Gender Distribution





Nearly balanced gender representation, 55 males, 48 females) minimizes sampling bias, as shown in Figure 2. This equilibrium supports gender-stratified analyses without confounding by disproportionate representation.


Survival Pattern Analysis:

Age-Survival Relationship:








Figure 3: Age Survival Relationship





Violin plots, Figure 3, demonstrates clear age-outcome divergences: recovered patients peak at 30-50 years while non-recovered concentrate above 60 years. Survival rates decline sharply: 87%, < 40 years, 57%, 40-60 years, and 24%, > 60 years.



Table 3: Survival percentages per Age Group
