| >60         |          24.1 |              75.9 |  29 |







Clinical Outcomes by Gender:

Gender-Survival Association:








Figure 4: Survival by Gender





Figure 4 shows proportional recovery rates (\(\pm\) 59% overall) identical across genders despite higher raw non-recovery counts among males.



Clinical Trajectory Metrics:

Hospital Length Stay:
Length of Stay (LOS), Figure 5, reveal shorter median stays for recovered patients versus prolonged stays for non-recovered cases, reflecting disease severity.








Figure 5: Length of Stay







Ventilation and Treatment Analysis:

Ventilated patients showed a 70% mortality rate vs 35% mortality rate for the non-ventilated patients.


Clinical Variable Intercorrelations:








Figure 6: Correlation Heatmap





The expanded heatmap, Figure 6, highlights strongest relationships: neutrophils - lymphocytes. Notable absent: age-outcome correlation due to categorical target encoding. Weak age associations with blood metrics suggest independent demographic effects.



Statistical Hypothesis Testing:


Gender-Survival Chi-square: χ²=2.68, p=0.1016


Age by Outcome T-test: t=-6.90, p=0.0000



Chi-square test for gender-survival association:
A Chi-square test of independence was performed to examine the relationship between patient gender and survival outcome.
The analysis produced \(x^2\) statistic of 2.68 with a corresponding p-value of 0.1016. Since the p-value is greater than the standard significance level of 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, that gender and survival are independent.
The statistical evidence suggests there is no significant association between a patient’s gender and their likelihood of recovery within this specific data-set. This supports the visual observation from Figure 2 , indicating similar proportional outcomes for both males and females.


T-Test for age difference by outcome:
An independent samples T-test was conducted to compare the mean age of patients who recovered versus those who did not recover.
The T-test yielded a T-statistic of -6.90 and an extremely low p-value. As the p-value is well below the 0.05 significance threshold, we reject the null hypothesis.
The negative T-statistic indicates that patients who recovered were, on average, younger than those who did not recover. This provides support for Figure 3 , highlighting age as a critical predictor of outcome in this cohort.

title: Using R and Python Together in Data Science
text:
TipLooking back (November 2026)



I wrote this in February 2026, early in learning to combine R and Python. Looking back, I scaled the data before splitting it into training and test sets, which lets information from the test set leak into training; scaling inside a scikit-learn Pipeline avoids that. With only 64 samples, a single 70/30 split also gives an unstable accuracy estimate, so cross-validation would be more reliable. And with over 22,000 genes, comparisons between groups need correcting for multiple testing. My second tutorial covers passing data between R and Python more carefully.

title: Using R and Python Together in Data Science
text:
Introduction:
The age old debate, which is better, R or Python? The answer is, it depends. Both languages have their strengths and weaknesses, and the best choice for a data scientist will depend on their specific needs and preferences. In this tutorial, we will explore the use of R and Python in data science.
In bioinformatics, we frequently encounter the ‘Curse of Dimensionality’ (the (pn) problem). Here, our dataset contains over 22,000 gene features but only 64 biological samples. Navigating this requires a bilingual approach: using Python’s scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) for efficient dimensionality reduction and R’s gtsummary (Sjoberg et al., 2021) for rigorous statistical validation.

Importing libraries, Modules and data:
The first library that needs to be imported, reticulate (Ushey, Allaire and Tang, 2025), is an R package that provides an interface to Python. It allows you to run Python code from R and to use Python libraries in R. The second library, tidyverse (Wickham et al., 2019), is a collection of R packages that are designed for data science. It includes packages for data manipulation, visualization, and modeling.
The python modules that need to be imported are pandas (team, 2020), numpy(Harris et al., 2020), matplotlib.pyplot(Hunter, 2007), and seaborn (Waskom, 2021). Pandas (team, 2020) is a library for data manipulation and analysis. It provides data structures and functions for working with structured data. Numpy (Harris et al., 2020) is a library for numerical computing. It provides functions for working with arrays and matrices. Matplotlib.pyplot (Hunter, 2007) is a library for creating static, animated, and interactive visualizations in Python. Seaborn (Waskom, 2021) is a library for making statistical graphics in Python. It is built on top of matplotlib (Hunter, 2007) and provides a high-level interface for drawing attractive and informative statistical graphics.

# Importing libraries
library(reticulate)
library(tidyverse)
library(ivo.table)
library(gtsummary)


# Importing modules
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import kagglehub
import os
from kagglehub import KaggleDatasetAdapter
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report



Import data from kaggle:
Data can be imported from Kaggle using the kagglehub library. The dataset_load() function is used to load a specific file from a Kaggle dataset. The handle of the dataset and the path to the specific file need to be provided as arguments to the function. This method avoids the DeprecationWarning that occurs when using the kaggle library directly.
The ‘magic’ of this workflow lies in the reticulate package (Ushey, Allaire and Tang, 2025). When we load data in a Python chunk, it is stored in the Python memory space. We can then access that exact same data in an R chunk using the py$ prefix (e.g., py$df). This allows for a seamless handover from data processing to statistical reporting without the need to export and re-import CSV files.

Data Availability & Attribution:
This analysis utilizes the Leukemia gene expression dataset from the Curated Microarray Database (CuMiDa). The data was accessed via Kaggle. This dataset is provided under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International license.


Python Kaggle Data Loading Code
# 1. Handle name: "user/dataset-slug"
handle = "brunogrisci/leukemia-gene-expression-cumida"
# 2. Specific file: ensure it matches the dataset's content
file_path = "Leukemia_GSE9476.csv"

# Use dataset_load() to avoid the DeprecationWarning
df = kagglehub.dataset_load(
    KaggleDatasetAdapter.PANDAS,
    handle=handle,
    path=file_path
)

rows = len(df)
columns = f'{len(df.columns):,}'

print(f"Data loaded successfully! Shape: {df.shape}")


Data loaded successfully! Shape: (64, 22285)


The dataset contains 64 samples and 22,285 columns, with the second column being the type of leukemia and the remaining columns representing gene expression levels. The dataset can be explored using the head() function to view the first few rows of the data.



Principal Component Analysis (PCA):
Before building a predictive model, we use Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to project these 22,000+ dimensions into 2D space. This helps us visualize whether the leukemia subtypes—such as AML versus Bone Marrow samples—naturally cluster together. If we see clear separation in the PCA plot, it provides biological confidence that a machine learning classifier will be successful.


Variance explained by top 2 components: 34.22%




PCA Plot
pca_data <- py$pca_df

ggplot(pca_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = Target)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha =  0.7) +
  labs(title = "PCA of Leukemia Gene Expression Data",
       x = "Principal Component 1",
       y = "Principal Component 2") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Set1')









The PCA plot shows the distribution of samples based on the first two principal components. Different colors represent different types of leukemia, allowing for visual assessment of how well the types are separated in the reduced dimensional space. I used reticulate to leverage Python’s robust data manipulation and machine learning libraries while utilizing R’s powerful visualization capabilities to create the PCA plot. This combination allows for efficient data processing and insightful visual representation of the results.

This was one of my first predictive models, built in February 2026. Today I would split the data by time, training on earlier years and testing on later ones, instead of splitting it randomly: a random split lets the model learn from the very years it is meant to predict. I would also describe the correlations as associations rather than “drivers”, and check the findings against the official WHO Global TB Report data before drawing conclusions. title: Global Tuberculosis Trends, 2000–2024
text:
Introduction:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant global health challenge, affecting millions of people worldwide, particularly in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. The World Health Organization (WHO) adopted a blueprint in 2014, the End TB Strategy, which aims to reduce incidence by 80% by the year 2030, using the year 2015 as a baseline.
This project conducts an exploratory data analysis (EDA) of the Tuberculosis_Trends.csv (Kyada, 2024) dataset available on Kaggle, which captures comprehensive country-level public health data from 2000 - 2024. The primary objective is to uncover patterns and relationships between TB indicators (cases, mortality, treatment success) and various socio-economic and health infrastructure metrics to identify key drivers of disease prevalence. Specifically, this analysis aims to answer:

How have TB cases and deaths trended in South Africa compared to other regions?
What socio-economic or health infrastructure factors show the strongest correlation with reduced TB burden?
Does the current trajectory indicate South Africa will meet the 2030 reduction targets?

title: Global Tuberculosis Trends, 2000–2024
text:
Conclusion and Actionable Recommendations:
This exploratory data analysis and predictive modeling project successfully identified key drivers of tuberculosis prevalence in South Africa and forecasted potential future trends. The analysis highlights that South Africa, under its current trajectory, is not projected to meet the ambitious 80% TB incidence reduction target by 2030.
Key Takeaways and Insights:

The strongest negative correlation was found between Access_To_Health_Services and TB_Deaths.
GDP_Per_Capita and TB_Treatment_Success_Rate were significant features in predicting TB cases, along with general population density.
The high variability of HIV co-infected cases highlights a need for better integrated screening and treatment programs.

Next Steps:
Future work will involve validating the insights found here by analyzing the official WHO Global TB Report dataset, as the current analysis utilizes a similar but separate dataset obtained via Kaggle. Additionally, future analysis could incorporate more granular geographic data to identify specific TB hotspots, perform cost-effectiveness analysis for the recommended interventions, or explore more advanced time-series models to refine long-term forecasting.
Limitations:

The analysis utilized a dataset obtained via Kaggle, which is similar to but separate from the official WHO Global TB Report dataset. Future work would involve validating these insights against the official WHO data.
The correlation analysis and predictive modeling were specifically conducted using data only for South Africa, limiting the immediate generalizability of these specific findings to other countries or regions.
Official death counts can be complex due to reporting issues (e.g., HIV and TB are often under-reported on death certificates), which may introduce some bias into the historical data.
While a Random Forest Regressor was used, future analysis could explore more advanced time-series models to refine long-term forecasting accuracy.

title: Using one dataset in both R and Python
text:
Why use both?
R and Python each have strengths. R has dplyr, ggplot2 and a deep set of statistics and Bioconductor packages; Python has pandas, scikit-learn and most machine learning tools. With reticulate, a single Quarto document (or R session) can run both languages and pass data between them, without saving and re-reading CSV files in between.

title: Using one dataset in both R and Python
text:
1. Set up reticulate
reticulate needs a Python installation with pandas. Using a project-specific environment keeps package versions stable. For example, with uv in your project folder:
uv init --bare
uv add pandas numpy
Then tell reticulate to use it, before any Python code runs:

library(reticulate)
use_python(here::here(".venv", "bin", "python"))   # on Windows: ".venv/Scripts/python.exe"

Check that reticulate found Python and pandas:

py_module_available("pandas")

[1] TRUE

py_version()

[1] '3.12'








Tip



Once Python has started in an R session, reticulate can’t switch to another Python. If it picked the wrong one, restart R (Session → Restart R) and call use_python() first. Setting the RETICULATE_PYTHON environment variable in your project’s .Renviron makes the choice permanent.

2. Prepare the data in R
Load the baseline table and the baseline-visit cell counts, as in Tutorial 1, and join them:

library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)
library(ggplot2)


missing_codes <- c("", "N/A", "ND", ".", "-", "not done")

baseline <- read_csv(baseline_path) |>
  distinct(pt_id, .keep_all = TRUE)            # two participants were entered twice

baseline_cells <- read_excel(cells_path, sheet = "Baseline", col_types = "text") |>
  type_convert(na = missing_codes) |>
  clean_names() |>
  select(pt_id, macrophages_percent, lymphocytes_percent, neutrophils_percent)

bal <- baseline |>
  left_join(baseline_cells, by = "pt_id") |>
  mutate(
    tb_diagnosis = factor(tb_diagnosis, levels = c("Control", "LTBI", "Active TB")),
    viability_percent = 100 * live_cells / total_cells
  ) |>
  select(pt_id, sex, tb_diagnosis, hiv_status, age_at_visit, bronc_date,

Two conversions need care, because neither raises an error.

Pitfall 1: integer columns with missing values
R stores a missing integer as a special number. pandas’ standard integer type has no way to represent “missing”, so that special number comes through as if it were a real value:

demo <- data.frame(minutes = c(120L, NA, 95L))   # 120L means "integer 120"
demo

1     120

3      95

0         120
1 -2147483648

The missing value became -2147483648, and any average you calculate in Python is now wrong. Convert integer columns to doubles in R before sending them:

demo <- demo |>
  mutate(across(where(is.integer), as.double))


r.demo

0    120.0
1      NaN
2     95.0








Tip



read_csv() and read_excel() read numbers as doubles, so you mainly meet this with columns you created with as.integer(), 1L or functions such as n().




Pitfall 2: dates
R Date columns arrive as a column of plain Python date objects (dtype object), not as pandas dates:

print(bal["bronc_date"].dtype)

object

print(type(bal["bronc_date"].iloc[0]))

<class 'datetime.date'>

bal["bronc_date"] = pd.to_datetime(bal["bronc_date"])
bal["bronc_year"] = bal["bronc_date"].dt.year

Going the other way, pandas datetimes come back to R as date-times (POSIXct), displayed in your computer’s time zone. Use as.Date() if you only need the date.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
NoteWhat you’ll learn




Choose a test from three questions: what kind of data, how many groups, and whether the measurements are paired
Check the assumptions a test relies on, with plots and the Shapiro-Wilk test
What each common test does, when to use it, and how to run it in R
Read the output: the test statistic, the p-value and the confidence interval
Measure how big a difference is (effect size), and check whether a study could have detected it (power)
Report a result in one clear sentence

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
1. Set up
Put the two cleaned files in your project’s data/ folder and load the packages. Every test in this tutorial is part of base R; the packages are for loading, reshaping and plotting the data.

library(readr)    # read the CSV files
library(dplyr)    # data manipulation
library(tidyr)    # reshape data for paired tests
library(ggplot2)  # plots
library(here)     # file paths from the project root


metadata_path <- here("data", "bal_metadata_clean.csv")
cells_path    <- here("data", "bal_cell_counts_clean.csv")

A CSV file stores categories as plain text, so set their order again after loading. Without this, R sorts them alphabetically and every table and plot starts with “Active TB”:

metadata <- read_csv(metadata_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    tb_diagnosis   = factor(tb_diagnosis, levels = c("Control", "LTBI", "Active TB", "Indeterminate")),
    hiv_status     = factor(hiv_status, levels = c("Negative", "Positive")),
    smoking_status = factor(smoking_status, levels = c("Never", "Former", "Current"))
  )

cell_counts <- read_csv(cells_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("Baseline", "Month3", "Month6", "Month12")))

# One row per participant: their details plus their baseline cell counts
baseline <- metadata |>
  inner_join(filter(cell_counts, visit == "Baseline"), by = "pt_id")

dim(baseline)

[1] 500  58

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
2. How to choose a test
Every test answers a version of the same question: could the pattern in this sample just be chance? The answer comes as a p-value.






TipReading a p-value



Every test starts by assuming there’s no real difference between the groups (or no real link between two variables). This starting assumption is called the null hypothesis. The p-value then asks:

If there were no real difference, how likely is it that chance alone would give a difference at least as big as the one in our data?


A small p-value (below 0.05) means a difference this big would rarely happen by chance alone. The data would be surprising if the null hypothesis were true, so we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there’s probably a real difference: the result is statistically significant.
A large p-value (0.05 or above) means a difference this big could easily happen by chance. The data gives no evidence of a real difference.

For example, p = 0.03 means that if there were no real difference, chance alone would produce a difference at least this large only about 3 times in 100.
The cut-off of 0.05 (1 in 20) is a convention, called the significance level and written α (alpha). Choose it before you look at the results, not after (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.4.3).
Three things a p-value doesn’t tell you:

How big or important the difference is. In a large study, even a tiny, unimportant difference can have a very small p-value. Always look at the means or medians too.
That the groups are the same. A large p-value means “we found no evidence of a difference”, not “there is no difference”. The study may simply be too small to tell.
The chance that the null hypothesis is true. It’s the chance of the data, assuming the null hypothesis is true, not the other way round.

Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.4.3) for hypothesis testing and p-values, and section 4.2 for confidence intervals (free PDF).


To choose a test, answer three questions about your data:

What kind of outcome is it? A measurement on a scale (BMI, cell percentages) or a category (HIV status, smear result)?
How many groups are you comparing? Two, or three or more?
Are the groups independent or paired? Different people in each group, or the same people measured twice?

For measurements, there’s a fourth: do the values roughly follow a normal (bell-shaped) distribution? Tests that assume this are called parametric. Their non-parametric alternatives work on the ranks of the values instead, so they don’t need it. The price is a little less power when the data really is normal: the Wilcoxon rank-sum test is about 95% as powerful as the t-test (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.8). So use the parametric test when its assumptions hold, and the rank-based one when they don’t.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
3. Check the assumptions first
The parametric tests assume the values in each group come from a roughly normal distribution. There are two ways to check.
Look at the data. A histogram shows the shape. A Q-Q plot (quantile-quantile plot) is more precise: it plots the values against what a normal distribution would give, so normal data falls along the straight line.

baseline |>
  select(bmi, neutrophils_percent) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "measurement", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "#E36414") +
  facet_wrap(~ measurement, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Expected if normal", y = "Observed") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Q-Q plots. BMI follows the line, so it’s close to normal. Neutrophil percentages curve away from it: most values are low, with a long tail of high values.





Test it. The Shapiro-Wilk test has the null hypothesis “these values come from a normal distribution”. A small p-value (below 0.05) is evidence that they don’t. Check each group separately, because the assumption applies to each group:

baseline |>
  filter(!is.na(bmi)) |>
  group_by(tb_diagnosis) |>
  summarise(n = n(), shapiro_p = shapiro.test(bmi)$p.value)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  tb_diagnosis      n shapiro_p
  <fct>         <int>     <dbl>
1 Control         108    0.926 
2 LTBI            153    0.0980
3 Active TB       163    0.350 
4 Indeterminate    73    0.153 


Every group has p above 0.05, so BMI looks normal in all four groups.






WarningDon’t rely on the Shapiro-Wilk test alone



With large groups, Shapiro-Wilk flags tiny departures from normality that don’t matter; with small groups, it misses big ones. Use it together with the plots, not instead of them. Look mainly for strong skew and outliers, the departures that cause real problems (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.1). And the t-test and ANOVA cope with mild non-normality once the groups are reasonably large.
The normal distribution, and how to judge whether data follows it with a Q-Q plot, are in Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.3.3) (free PDF).

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
4. Comparing two groups

Welch’s t-test






NoteAbout Welch’s t-test



What it does: compares the means of a measurement in two independent groups. It divides the difference between the two sample means by its standard error, the amount that difference would vary by chance from one sample to the next. The further this t statistic is from 0, the less likely the difference is to be chance.
Use it when: the outcome is a numeric measurement, there are two groups of different people, and the values in each group look roughly normal.
Assumptions, most important first (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.13.2):

Independent observations. Each person appears once, and one person’s value doesn’t affect another’s. This matters most: even mild dependence makes p-values too small, and only the study design can tell you whether it holds.
A numeric measurement, not a category or a score.
Roughly normal values in each group. Check each group on its own, not the combined data. The test copes with mild departures in larger samples: about 30 or more per group (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.1), and comfortably above 100 (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.13.2).

The classic Student’s t-test also assumes the two groups have the same spread (variance). Welch’s version doesn’t, which is why R uses it by default. When the spreads really are equal, Student’s test is only slightly more powerful, so Welch’s is the safer choice (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.13.2).
In R: t.test(outcome ~ group, data = ...)
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.5.3) (free PDF); chapter 13 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021).


Question: do participants with active TB have a different BMI from controls? BMI looked normal in every group (section 3), so a t-test fits. Keep just the two groups, then run it:

two_groups <- baseline |>
  filter(tb_diagnosis %in% c("Active TB", "Control")) |>
  mutate(tb_diagnosis = droplevels(tb_diagnosis))

t.test(bmi ~ tb_diagnosis, data = two_groups)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  bmi by tb_diagnosis
t = -1.5653, df = 255.13, p-value = 0.1187
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Control and group Active TB is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.4970072  0.2853734
sample estimates:
  mean in group Control mean in group Active TB 
               24.25185                25.35767 


How to read it:

mean in group: the average BMI in each group, about 24.3 in controls and 25.4 with active TB.
t and df: the test statistic and its degrees of freedom. You report them, but the p-value is what you interpret.
p-value: 0.12, above 0.05, so there’s no evidence that mean BMI differs between the groups.
95 percent confidence interval: the range of plausible values for the difference in means. It includes 0 (no difference), which matches the p-value.

droplevels() matters here: after filtering, tb_diagnosis still knows about the LTBI and Indeterminate levels, and t.test() needs exactly two.


Wilcoxon rank-sum test






NoteAbout the Wilcoxon rank-sum test



What it does: compares two independent groups using the ranks of the values instead of the values themselves. All the values from both groups are put in order and numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. If one group’s values tend to be larger, its ranks add up to more than you’d expect by chance (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.2). It’s also called the Mann-Whitney U test.
Use it when: there are two groups of different people, and the outcome is skewed, has outliers, comes from small groups, or is an ordered score (such as a smear grade) rather than a measurement.
Assumptions: rank-based tests make weaker assumptions than the t-test, but they aren’t assumption-free (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.1 and 33.5):

Independent observations, as for the t-test.
An outcome you can put in order: a measurement or an ordered score, not a plain category.
Distributions of a similar shape in the two groups, apart from where they’re centred. When that holds, the test compares the medians. When it doesn’t, a significant result only tells you that values in one group tend to be larger, not that the medians differ.

The trade-off: if the data really is normal, the test is about 95% as powerful as the t-test (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.8). That’s why the t-test is still the first choice when its assumptions hold.
In R: wilcox.test(outcome ~ group, data = ...)
Read more: section 33.5 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021), and R’s wilcox.test help page (or type ?wilcox.test in the console). For a related approach that also avoids assuming normality, a randomisation test, see chapter 20 of Çetinkaya-Rundel and Hardin (2024).


Question: do neutrophil percentages differ between active TB and latent TB infection (LTBI)? Section 3 showed neutrophil percentages are strongly skewed, so use the rank-based test. Plot first, then test:

active_vs_ltbi <- baseline |>
  filter(tb_diagnosis %in% c("Active TB", "LTBI")) |>
  mutate(tb_diagnosis = droplevels(tb_diagnosis))

ggplot(active_vs_ltbi, aes(tb_diagnosis, neutrophils_percent)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Neutrophils (%)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 2: Neutrophil percentage at baseline in latent TB infection and active TB.






active_vs_ltbi |>
  group_by(tb_diagnosis) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(neutrophils_percent)),
            median = median(neutrophils_percent, na.rm = TRUE))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  tb_diagnosis     n median
  <fct>        <int>  <dbl>
1 LTBI           151    1.8
2 Active TB      157   19.5

wilcox.test(neutrophils_percent ~ tb_diagnosis, data = active_vs_ltbi, exact = FALSE)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  neutrophils_percent by tb_diagnosis
W = 0, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


The median neutrophil percentage is about 2% with LTBI and about 20% with active TB, and the p-value is far below 0.05: strong evidence of a difference.
Check the shape assumption against the plot: the LTBI values are tightly bunched near 2%, while the active TB values are spread widely. The shapes aren’t similar, so the safe conclusion is that neutrophil percentages tend to be higher in active TB, rather than a precise statement about medians.
W is the test statistic: the number of pairs, one person from each group, in which the first group’s value (here LTBI, the first level) is the larger. W = 0 means that in every possible pair, the person with active TB had the higher neutrophil percentage: the two groups don’t overlap at all, as the plot shows. That clean separation is a feature of this simulated data. exact = FALSE tells R to use the normal approximation, which is standard when there are tied values or more than about 50 observations.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
5. Comparing three or more groups
You might be tempted to run a t-test on every pair of groups. With four groups that’s six tests, and each one has a 5% chance of a false positive, so the chance of at least one false alarm climbs to about 26% (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.5). Instead, test all the groups at once.

One-way ANOVA






NoteAbout one-way ANOVA



What it does: analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests whether three or more independent groups all have the same mean. It splits the total variation in the outcome into two parts: variation between the group means, and variation within each group, from person to person. The F statistic is the ratio of the two. If the group means are further apart than the person-to-person variation would explain, F is large and the p-value small (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.17.3).
Use it when: the outcome is a numeric measurement, there are three or more groups of different people, and the values in each group look roughly normal.
Assumptions (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.5):

Independent observations, within and across the groups.
Roughly normal values in each group. As with the t-test, ANOVA copes with mild departures when the groups are reasonably large.
Similar spread in each group. Compare the boxes in a boxplot, or the groups’ standard deviations.

In R: aov(outcome ~ group, data = ...), then summary() on the result.
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.5.5) (free PDF), which also covers the multiple-comparisons problem; chapters 17 and 18 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021).


Question: does BMI differ across the four diagnosis groups? BMI looked normal in all four, so use ANOVA:

bmi_anova <- aov(bmi ~ tb_diagnosis, data = baseline)
summary(bmi_anova)

              Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
tb_diagnosis   3    265   88.28   2.083  0.102
Residuals    493  20890   42.37               
3 observations deleted due to missingness


The row that matters is tb_diagnosis. F value is the test statistic (between-group variation divided by within-group variation), and Pr(>F) is the p-value: 0.10. So there’s no evidence that mean BMI differs across the four groups.






Tip



A significant ANOVA tells you that at least one group differs, not which one. Finding out which groups differ needs a post hoc test, which is in Tutorial 5.




Kruskal-Wallis test






NoteAbout the Kruskal-Wallis test



What it does: the rank-based version of one-way ANOVA. It ranks all the values across the groups, then tests whether the average rank differs between groups (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.6). With two groups it gives the same answer as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
Use it when: there are three or more groups of different people, and the outcome is skewed, has outliers, comes from small groups, or is an ordered score.
Assumptions: the same as the Wilcoxon rank-sum test: independent observations, an outcome you can put in order, and distributions of a similar shape in every group. Similar skew matters most: if one group is strongly skewed and another isn’t, a significant result is hard to interpret (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.6).
The trade-off: it’s less informative than ANOVA. A significant result says the groups differ, but working out which ones is harder (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.8). Tutorial 5 covers the follow-up tests.
In R: kruskal.test(outcome ~ group, data = ...)
Read more: section 33.6 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021), and R’s kruskal.test help page. For a randomisation approach to comparing many groups, see chapter 22 of Çetinkaya-Rundel and Hardin (2024).


Question: do macrophage percentages differ across the diagnosis groups? Cell percentages are skewed, so use Kruskal-Wallis:

ggplot(baseline, aes(tb_diagnosis, macrophages_percent)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Macrophages (%)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 3: Macrophage percentage at baseline by TB diagnosis.






kruskal.test(macrophages_percent ~ tb_diagnosis, data = baseline)


    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  macrophages_percent by tb_diagnosis
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 390.9, df = 3, p-value < 2.2e-16


The p-value is extremely small: macrophage percentages clearly differ between the diagnosis groups. The plot shows where: participants with active TB have far fewer macrophages, because more of their BAL cells are lymphocytes and neutrophils. df is the number of groups minus one.
As with the Wilcoxon example, the groups’ shapes aren’t identical: the active TB values are much more spread out. So read this as “macrophage percentages tend to be lower in active TB”, and use the follow-up tests in Tutorial 5 to compare specific groups.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
6. Paired measurements

Paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test






NoteAbout paired tests



What they do: compare two measurements taken on the same participants, such as before and after treatment. Instead of comparing two groups, they work out each person’s change and test whether the changes are centred on zero.
Use them when: each value in one set has a partner in the other: the same person at two visits, two samples from the same patient, or matched pairs.
Why pairing helps: people differ a lot from one another. Comparing each person with themselves removes that person-to-person variation, so a paired test can detect much smaller changes (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.20.2). Treating paired data as two independent groups is a common mistake, and it can hide a real effect (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.3).
Assumptions:

Paired t-test: the pairs are independent of each other, and the differences are roughly normal. The original values don’t need to be normal, and differences are often close to normal even when the values aren’t (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.20.3).
Wilcoxon signed-rank test: the pairs are independent, and the differences are roughly symmetric around their centre, though not necessarily normal (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.4).

How R pairs the values: given two vectors, R pairs them by position: the first value with the first, the second with the second (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.20.4). Make sure each row holds one person’s two measurements, as pivot_wider() does below.
In R: t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE) or wilcox.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.5.2) (free PDF) and chapter 20 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021) for the paired t-test; section 33.4 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021) for the Wilcoxon signed-rank test; chapter 21 of Çetinkaya-Rundel and Hardin (2024) for a randomisation version.


Question: in participants with active TB, does the neutrophil percentage change between baseline and month 6? Put each participant’s two visits side by side with pivot_wider(), keeping only people with both:

neutrophils_paired <- cell_counts |>
  filter(visit %in% c("Baseline", "Month6")) |>
  inner_join(select(metadata, pt_id, tb_diagnosis), by = "pt_id") |>
  filter(tb_diagnosis == "Active TB") |>
  select(pt_id, visit, neutrophils_percent) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = neutrophils_percent) |>
  filter(!is.na(Baseline), !is.na(Month6)) |>
  mutate(change = Month6 - Baseline)

nrow(neutrophils_paired)

[1] 85


Check the assumption on the differences:

shapiro.test(neutrophils_paired$change)


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  neutrophils_paired$change
W = 0.98904, p-value = 0.6974


The differences look normal (p above 0.05), so the paired t-test fits:

t.test(neutrophils_paired$Month6, neutrophils_paired$Baseline, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  neutrophils_paired$Month6 and neutrophils_paired$Baseline
t = -5.7087, df = 84, p-value = 1.672e-07
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -5.975552 -2.887978
sample estimates:
mean difference 
      -4.431765 


The mean difference is negative: on average, neutrophil percentages fell by about 4 percentage points between baseline and month 6, and the confidence interval doesn’t include 0. The p-value is very small. The order of the two arguments sets the sign: Month6 first gives month 6 minus baseline.
If the differences hadn’t been normal, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test would be the choice. It reaches the same conclusion here:

wilcox.test(neutrophils_paired$Month6, neutrophils_paired$Baseline, paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)


    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  neutrophils_paired$Month6 and neutrophils_paired$Baseline
V = 702.5, p-value = 8.333e-07
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
7. Two categorical variables

Chi-square test of independence






NoteAbout the chi-square test



What it does: tests whether two categorical variables are associated: whether knowing one tells you something about the other. Assuming there’s no association, it works out the count you’d expect in each cell of the table: the row total times the column total, divided by the overall total (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.8.3). The chi-square statistic adds up how far each observed count is from its expected count. The bigger the mismatch, the smaller the p-value.
Use it when: both variables are categories (HIV status, smear result) and each person is counted once.
Assumptions:

Independent observations. Each person falls in exactly one cell. That rules out, for example, before-and-after measurements on the same people (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.32.2).
Large enough expected counts, checked on the expected counts, not the observed ones. The rules of thumb differ: at least 5 in every cell (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.32.2), or more cautiously at least 10 (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.8.3). Below that, the p-value isn’t reliable: use Fisher’s exact test instead.

In R: chisq.test(table(variable_1, variable_2))
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.8.3) (free PDF); chapter 32 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021).


Question: among people with active TB, is a negative sputum smear more common in people living with HIV? Make the table first:

active_tb <- baseline |>
  filter(tb_diagnosis == "Active TB") |>
  mutate(smear = if_else(smear_grade == "Negative", "Smear negative", "Smear positive"))

smear_hiv <- table(active_tb$smear, active_tb$hiv_status)
smear_hiv

                
                 Negative Positive
  Smear negative       17       24
  Smear positive       81       42


Check the expected counts, then run the test:

smear_test <- chisq.test(smear_hiv)
smear_test$expected

                
                 Negative Positive
  Smear negative     24.5     16.5
  Smear positive     73.5     49.5

smear_test


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  smear_hiv
X-squared = 6.6263, df = 1, p-value = 0.01005


Every expected count is above 10, so the test is valid by either rule of thumb. The p-value is below 0.05: smear results and HIV status are associated. The table shows the direction: 24 of 66 people living with HIV had a negative smear (36%), against 17 of 98 HIV-negative people (17%).
For a 2×2 table, R applies Yates’ continuity correction by default, which makes the test slightly more cautious. That’s why the output says “with Yates’ continuity correction”.


Fisher’s exact test






NoteAbout Fisher’s exact test



What it does: answers the same question as the chi-square test, whether two categorical variables are associated. Instead of an approximation that needs large counts, it calculates the p-value exactly, from every way the counts could have been arranged given the table’s row and column totals.
Use it when: the expected counts are too small for the chi-square test: below 5, or below 10 by the more cautious rule (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.8.3). It’s usually used for 2×2 tables. R can run it on larger tables, but the calculation gets heavy.
Assumptions: independent observations. There’s no minimum count.
In R: fisher.test(table(variable_1, variable_2))
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.8.3) (free PDF).


Question: among people with TB detected by GeneXpert, is rifampicin-resistant TB more common in children (under 18)?

tb_detected <- metadata |>
  filter(gene_xpert_rif %in% c("Resistant", "Sensitive")) |>
  mutate(age_group = if_else(age < 18, "Under 18", "18 and over"))

rif_age <- table(tb_detected$gene_xpert_rif, tb_detected$age_group)
rif_age

           
            18 and over Under 18
  Resistant          20        2
  Sensitive          90       14


Only 16 children had TB detected, and only 2 had resistant TB. Try the chi-square test and R warns you:

chisq.test(rif_age)$expected

Warning in chisq.test(rif_age): Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect


           
            18 and over  Under 18
  Resistant    19.20635  2.793651
  Sensitive    90.79365 13.206349

chisq.test(rif_age)

Warning in chisq.test(rif_age): Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect



    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  rif_age
X-squared = 0.042836, df = 1, p-value = 0.836


The expected count for resistant TB in children is below 5 (about 2.8), so the chi-square p-value can’t be trusted by either rule of thumb. Use Fisher’s exact test:

fisher.test(rif_age)


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  rif_age
p-value = 0.7361
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
  0.3149951 15.1391900
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
   1.55063 


The p-value is 0.74: no evidence that resistance is more or less common in children. Fisher’s test also reports an odds ratio with a confidence interval. The interval is very wide (it runs from well below 1 to well above it), which is what small numbers look like: the data is compatible with anything from much lower to much higher odds of resistance in children.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
8. Two measurements: correlation






NoteAbout correlation



What it does: measures how strongly two measurements on the same people move together, as a coefficient from −1 to +1. Near +1: when one is high, so is the other. Near −1: when one is high, the other is low. Near 0: no relationship. cor.test() also tests whether the coefficient differs from zero.
Pearson’s r measures a straight-line (linear) relationship. Its assumptions (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.14.1):

Both variables are numeric measurements.
Both are roughly normal; this matters for the p-value.
The relationship is linear: the scatter plot looks like a line, not a curve. It’s also sensitive to outliers, so always plot first.

Spearman’s rho is Pearson’s r calculated on the ranks. It measures whether one variable tends to rise (or fall) as the other rises, in a straight line or not: a monotonic relationship. It works for skewed data and ordered scores. Its assumptions (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.7):

Both variables can be put in order.
The relationship is monotonic. Don’t use it if the scatter plot forms a hill or a valley.

When Pearson’s assumptions do hold, Spearman’s is somewhat less powerful (roughly 91% in some evaluations) (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.33.7).
In R: cor.test(x, y, method = "pearson") or cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")
Read more: correlation and scatterplots in Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.1.6 and 6.1) (free PDF) and chapter 14 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021). For Spearman’s rho, see section 33.7 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021) and R’s cor.test help page.


Question: do people with a stronger IGRA response have more lymphocytes in their BAL fluid? Plot it first, as always:

ggplot(baseline, aes(igra_value_iu_ml, lymphocytes_percent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "IGRA value (IU/ml)", y = "Lymphocytes (%)") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 4: IGRA value and baseline lymphocyte percentage. Both are skewed, with many low values and a few high ones.





Both variables are skewed, so Spearman is the right choice. Running both shows how they compare:

cor.test(baseline$igra_value_iu_ml, baseline$lymphocytes_percent, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)


    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  baseline$igra_value_iu_ml and baseline$lymphocytes_percent
S = 9958014, p-value = 1.836e-15
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
      rho 
0.3615035 

cor.test(baseline$igra_value_iu_ml, baseline$lymphocytes_percent, method = "pearson")


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  baseline$igra_value_iu_ml and baseline$lymphocytes_percent
t = 6.8878, df = 452, p-value = 1.907e-11
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2224856 0.3891957
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.3082049 


Spearman’s rho is about 0.36: a weak-to-moderate positive relationship, very unlikely to be chance (p far below 0.05). Pearson’s r is a little lower because the relationship isn’t a straight line. cor.test() drops participants with a missing value in either variable automatically.






WarningCorrelation is not causation



This association doesn’t mean a stronger IGRA response causes more lymphocytes, or the reverse. In this dataset, both are highest in participants with active TB, so TB diagnosis may drive both. A third variable behind an association is called a confounder; regression, in Tutorial 5, is one way to account for it.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
section: 9. How big is the difference? Effect size and power
text:
9. How big is the difference? Effect size and power
A p-value tells you whether a difference is likely to be real, not whether it matters. Statistical significance isn’t the same as biological or clinical importance. In one river study, water pH differed significantly between open water and weed beds (p < 0.01), but the means were 7.1 and 6.9: a real difference, and almost certainly an unimportant one (Childs, Hindle and Warren, 2021, sec.10.3). Two more ideas complete the picture: effect size (how big is it?) and power (could the study have found it?).

Effect size






NoteAbout effect size



What it is: a measure of how big a difference or association is. Unlike a p-value, it doesn’t shrink just because the study is large.
In the original units: the difference between the group means (or medians), with its 95% confidence interval. This is usually the most useful version, because readers can judge directly whether it matters: is a difference of 1 kg/m² in BMI important? The confidence interval shows the range of differences the data is compatible with (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.4.2).
Standardised: Cohen’s d is the difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation, so it’s measured in standard deviations. That lets you compare effects across measurements with different units. Cohen’s rough guide is 0.2 for a small effect, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large (Cohen, 1988), but what counts as important depends on the measurement and the setting.
Correlations are already effect sizes: Pearson’s r and Spearman’s rho measure how strong a relationship is.
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.4.2) (free PDF) on confidence intervals; section 10.3 of Childs, Hindle and Warren (2021) on biological versus statistical significance.


Go back to the BMI comparison from section 4. t.test() already gives the effect size in the original units: the difference in means and its confidence interval. Cohen’s d takes a few lines:

bmi_summary <- two_groups |>
  filter(!is.na(bmi)) |>
  group_by(tb_diagnosis) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(bmi), sd = sd(bmi))
bmi_summary

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  tb_diagnosis     n  mean    sd
  <fct>        <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Control        108  24.3  5.25
2 Active TB      163  25.4  6.30

# Difference in means (active TB minus control)
difference <- diff(bmi_summary$mean)

# Pooled standard deviation: the two groups' SDs combined, weighted by group size
pooled_sd <- with(bmi_summary, sqrt(sum((n - 1) * sd^2) / (sum(n) - 2)))

c(difference = difference, pooled_sd = pooled_sd, cohens_d = difference / pooled_sd)

difference  pooled_sd   cohens_d 
 1.1058169  5.9064981  0.1872204 


Active TB participants averaged about 1.1 kg/m² more than controls, a Cohen’s d of about 0.19: a small effect, smaller than the person-to-person spread of almost 6 kg/m². The t-test’s confidence interval (section 4) runs from about 2.5 kg/m² lower to 0.3 kg/m² higher in controls, so the data is compatible with no difference or with a modest one.


Power






NoteAbout power



Two ways to be wrong: a test can find a difference that isn’t real (a Type I error, a false positive), or miss one that is (a Type II error, a false negative). The significance level, α = 0.05, is the chance of a Type I error (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.4.3).
What power is: the probability that a test detects a real effect of a given size, if it exists (Çetinkaya-Rundel and Hardin, 2024, chap.14). Power is 1 minus the chance of a Type II error.
What it depends on: the size of the effect (bigger effects are easier to find), the variability of the measurement, the sample size, and α.
Use it when:

Planning a study: choose a sample size large enough to detect the smallest difference that would matter. Studies usually aim for 80% or 90% power, and the calculated sample size is always rounded up (Vu and Harrington, 2020, sec.5.4).
Reading a non-significant result: if the study had little power to detect an important difference, “no evidence of a difference” may just mean “too small to tell”.

Base the calculation on the smallest difference that would matter, not on the difference you happened to observe.
In R: power.t.test() for comparing two means (power.prop.test() for two proportions). Give it all but one of n (per group), delta (the difference), sd, sig.level and power, and it calculates the missing one.
Read more: Vu and Harrington (2020, sec.5.4) (free PDF), a worked example of power and sample size for a clinical trial; chapter 14 of Çetinkaya-Rundel and Hardin (2024); R’s power.t.test help page.


Was the BMI comparison large enough to find a difference? power.t.test() assumes equal group sizes, so use the smaller group (108 controls); that errs on the cautious side. First, the smallest difference the study had an 80% chance of detecting:

power.t.test(n = 108, sd = pooled_sd, power = 0.80)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 108
          delta = 2.26202
             sd = 5.906498
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


delta is about 2.3 kg/m². Now the other way round: the power to detect a difference of 1 kg/m², about the size seen here:

power.t.test(n = 108, delta = 1, sd = pooled_sd)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 108
          delta = 1
             sd = 5.906498
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.2353285
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


Only about 24%. And the number per group that would give 80% power to detect 1 kg/m²:

power.t.test(delta = 1, sd = pooled_sd, power = 0.80)


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 548.6053
          delta = 1
             sd = 5.906498
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


About 549 per group, rounded up: five times as many as this study has. Putting it together: the study had a good chance of detecting a difference of about 2.3 kg/m² or more, and the confidence interval rules out differences much larger than 2.5 kg/m². But a smaller difference, like the 1.1 kg/m² seen here, can’t be ruled out: the study was too small to tell. That’s the practical meaning of “no evidence of a difference” from section 2.

title: Choosing and running statistical tests in R
text:
10. Report a result
A result needs more than “p < 0.05”. Report what was compared, the summary values, the test, the statistic and the p-value, in one sentence:

Median baseline neutrophil percentage was higher in active TB than in latent TB infection (median 19.5% vs 1.8%; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, W = 0, p < 0.001; n = 157 and 151).

Some conventions:

Give exact p-values to two significant figures (p = 0.12), and “p < 0.001” for anything smaller.
Report means with a t-test or ANOVA, and medians with the rank-based tests.
Report the size of the difference with its confidence interval, not just whether it’s significant.
Say how many people were in each group, and how many were left out because of missing values.

Common pitfalls








Problem
Symptom
Fix




Choosing the test after seeing the results
Trying tests until one gives p < 0.05
Choose the test from the data type and design, before testing


Many pairwise t-tests
False positives across lots of comparisons

Real changes look non-significant

R warns “approximation may be incorrect”

droplevels() after filtering

Most of my day happens in a terminal. Bioinformatics tools such as GATK and Nextflow have no buttons to click: you run them by typing commands. The same is true on a remote server or computing cluster, where the terminal is often the only way in. And even at my own desk, a few short commands answer “what’s in this file?” faster than opening it.
The command line looks unfriendly at first, but you need surprisingly little of it to be useful. This article covers the commands I use every day on Ubuntu, in the order you’d need them:
The last two sections use the simulated BAL dataset from my tutorial series, so you can follow along and check your output against mine.

title: The command line for biologists
text:
1. Open a terminal
The commands here are for Bash, the shell (command interpreter) on Ubuntu and most Linux systems.

Ubuntu and other Linux: press Ctrl + Alt + T, or search for “Terminal”.
macOS: open Terminal from Applications → Utilities. Its default shell is zsh rather than Bash, but every command in this article works the same in both.
Windows: install the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), which runs a real Linux system inside Windows. Open PowerShell as administrator (right-click → Run as administrator), run the command below, then restart (Microsoft, 2025):

wsl --install
It installs Ubuntu by default. Afterwards, open Ubuntu from the Start menu and you have the same terminal I use, so everything below applies as written. Your Windows drives are inside it too: C:\Users\you\Documents is /mnt/c/Users/you/Documents.
When the terminal opens you’ll see a prompt like devon@laptop:~$: your user name, the computer’s name, the folder you’re in (~ means your home folder), and a $ waiting for a command.

title: The command line for biologists
text:
2. Move around
Your files live in a tree of folders (also called directories). The terminal is always “in” one of them, the working directory, and commands act on files there unless you say otherwise.
pwd                 # print working directory: where am I?
ls                  # list what's here
ls -lh              # long list: sizes (human-readable), dates, permissions
ls -a               # include hidden files (names starting with .)
To move, use cd (change directory):
cd Documents        # into a folder inside the current one
cd Documents/bal    # several levels at once
cd ..               # up one level, to the parent folder
cd ~                # home folder (plain `cd` does the same)
cd -                # back to wherever you were before
cd /mnt/c/Users     # an absolute path: starts from the root, /
A path that starts with / is absolute: it means the same place wherever you are. Any other path is relative to the working directory. . means “here” and .. means “the folder above”.






TipLet the shell type for you



Press Tab while typing a file or folder name and the shell completes it; press it twice to see every match. It saves typing and catches typos, because it only completes names that exist. Up arrow brings back previous commands, and Ctrl + C stops a command that’s running (or abandons the line you’re typing).

title: The command line for biologists
text:
3. Create, copy, move and delete
mkdir bal-analysis              # make a folder
mkdir -p bal-analysis/data/raw  # make a whole path, parents included
touch notes.txt                 # make an empty file (or update its date)
Copy with cp, giving the source first and the destination second:
cp bal_baseline.csv backup.csv          # copy to a new name
cp bal_baseline.csv bal-analysis/data/  # copy into a folder, same name
cp -r bal-analysis bal-analysis-copy    # copy a folder and everything in it
Move or rename with mv. It’s the same command for both, because renaming is moving a file to a new name:
mv notes.txt bal-analysis/             # move into a folder
mv backup.csv bal_baseline_backup.csv  # rename
Delete with rm:
rm bal_baseline_backup.csv   # delete a file
rmdir empty-folder           # delete a folder, only if it's empty
rm -r bal-analysis-copy      # delete a folder and everything in it






WarningThere is no recycle bin



rm deletes immediately and permanently, and cp and mv silently overwrite a file that already has the destination name. Until it’s habit:

add -i (rm -i, cp -i, mv -i) to be asked before anything is deleted or overwritten;
run ls with the same name first (ls bal-analysis-copy) to see exactly what the command will touch;
be most careful with rm -r and with *, which matches every name in a folder.

Names with spaces need quotes (cd "My Documents"), which is one reason to name files with hyphens or underscores instead.


To read a whole text file, cat file.txt prints it, and less file.txt opens it one screen at a time (arrow keys or Space to scroll, / to search, q to quit). man ls opens the manual for any command, and most commands also accept --help.

title: The command line for biologists
section: 4. Install software and set up environments
text:
4. Install software and set up environments

System software: apt
On Ubuntu, most general software comes from the system’s package manager, apt. Installing for the whole system needs administrator rights, which is what sudo (“superuser do”) gives a single command; it asks for your password.
sudo apt update                  # refresh the list of available packages
sudo apt upgrade                 # install updates for everything installed
sudo apt install git curl tree   # install packages by name


Project environments
An environment is a separate set of packages for one project, kept apart from the rest of the computer, with a file that lists exactly which versions it holds. Setting one up takes a few minutes and saves a lot of trouble later:

Projects don’t break each other. Different tools need different versions of the same packages. Install everything in one place and adding a tool for a new project can quietly upgrade, downgrade or remove something an older project relies on. Sometimes the installer avoids a clash without telling you: when I added SRA Toolkit to my existing bioinformatics environment, it installed cleanly, but as a version from 2019, the newest that fitted alongside everything else. Asking for the current version would have downgraded Perl and removed another tool I use (regenie). A separate environment can hold the current version without touching anything.
Your results can be reproduced. The environment’s file records the version of every package, so you, a colleague or a reviewer can rebuild the same set-up next year and get the same answer. A package update that changes a default can otherwise change your results without any error.
Sharing a project is simple. Send the code with the environment file, and one command installs everything it needs on another computer.
The system stays safe. Environments live in your own folders and need no sudo, so they can’t break the software Ubuntu itself depends on, and you can delete one and rebuild it if something goes wrong.

Bioinformatics tools with micromamba. Many command-line bioinformatics tools (samtools, bwa, FastQC and thousands more) are packaged by Bioconda (Grüning et al., 2018), which installs through the conda family of package managers. I use micromamba: a single small program that does the same job as conda, solves installs quickly, and needs no base Python installation. Install it with the command from its documentation, and accept the suggested settings when it asks:
"${SHELL}" <(curl -L micro.mamba.pm)
Close and reopen the terminal, then tell it where to find packages. This one-time set-up uses the free conda-forge channel first and Bioconda second, as Bioconda recommends:
micromamba config append channels conda-forge
micromamba config append channels bioconda
micromamba config set channel_priority strict
Then create an environment for a project:
micromamba create -n qc fastqc samtools   # a new environment called qc, with two tools
micromamba activate qc                    # use it (the prompt shows (qc))
micromamba deactivate                     # leave it
To share an environment, or rebuild it later, export its list of packages to a file and create a new environment from that file:
micromamba env export -n qc > qc.yml      # write the environment's packages and versions to qc.yml
micromamba create -n qc2 -f qc.yml        # build an identical environment from the file
Run a tool from another environment without switching. When you’re working in one environment and need a single tool from another, micromamba run runs one command inside the other environment and leaves your current one active. There’s no need to deactivate, activate the other, run the tool, deactivate again and reactivate the first:
micromamba run -n qc fastqc reads_1.fastq.gz   # run FastQC from the qc environment
micromamba run -n qc samtools --version        # check a tool's version there
It’s also handy in scripts, which can call tools from several environments in turn.






Warningmicromamba run covers one command, not a whole pipe



micromamba run applies to the command straight after it; everything after a | runs in your normal shell. So in this pipe, the second samtools isn’t found, because it’s only installed in the qc environment:
micromamba run -n qc samtools view -h sample.bam | samtools view -c -
Command 'samtools' not found, but can be installed with:
…
Ubuntu suggests installing it with apt, but you don’t need to: it’s already in the environment, just not in the shell running that part of the pipe. For a pipe of tools from one environment, activate the environment first, or run the whole line inside it with bash -c:
micromamba run -n qc bash -c 'samtools view -h sample.bam | samtools view -c -'








Noteconda, mamba or micromamba?



All three install the same packages from the same channels, and their commands match: swap micromamba for conda or mamba in every command here (conda create, conda activate, conda run and so on). If you already have one of them, keep it. Many people also add alias mamba=micromamba to their ~/.bashrc so that instructions written for mamba work as they are.


Keep one environment per project or pipeline rather than installing everything into one. Before adding a package to an existing environment, micromamba install --dry-run lists what it would change, including the version it would install. If it would downgrade or remove anything, or picks an old version of the tool you asked for, make a new environment instead.
Pipelines build on the same idea: my variant-calling pipeline runs its tools from an environment with a single nextflow run command.

title: The command line for biologists
section: 5. Look at a data file without opening it
text:
5. Look at a data file without opening it
Now some real work. Download the messy baseline table from the tutorials into a folder, and cd into it. You can download it from the terminal too:
curl -O https://devonallies.co.za/tutorials/data/bal_baseline.csv
curl -O saves a web address to a file of the same name. Every command from here on runs in the folder holding bal_baseline.csv, and the output is what the file gives.






ImportantSimulated data



bal_baseline.csv is simulated: 500 fictional participants with TB diagnosis, HIV status and BAL cell counts. No row describes a real person. Tutorial 1 reads the same file into R.



How big is it, and what’s in it?

wc -l bal_baseline.csv

503 bal_baseline.csv


wc -l counts lines: 503, so one header row and 502 data rows. That’s two more rows than the 500 participants, which is worth remembering. head shows the start of the file:

head -n 3 bal_baseline.csv

pt_id,sex,tb_diagnosis,hiv_status,age_at_visit,bronc_date,dr_name,vol_pbs_in_ml,vol_pbs_out_ml,lobe,lab_tech,pellet_colour,live_cells,dead_cells,total_cells,time_to_process_min,diff_method
SP34696,Female,LTBI,Negative,53,2018-07-01,Dr. Van Der Merwe,100,45.7,Left Lower,thandi,Bloody,5432000,1169209,6601209,183,Manual
SP22845,Female,Control,Positive,30,2020-04-16,Dr. Naidoo,120,75.8,Left Upper,lize,Cream,3290000,1078335,4370000,124,Automated


Wide files are hard to read like that. head -n 1 takes just the header row, tr (translate) swaps each comma for a new line, and nl numbers the lines, giving a numbered list of the columns:

head -n 1 bal_baseline.csv | tr ',' '\n' | nl

     1  pt_id
     2  sex
     3  tb_diagnosis
     4  hiv_status
     5  age_at_visit
     6  bronc_date
     7  dr_name
     8  vol_pbs_in_ml
     9  vol_pbs_out_ml
    10  lobe
    11  lab_tech
    12  pellet_colour
    13  live_cells
    14  dead_cells
    15  total_cells
    16  time_to_process_min
    17  diff_method


The | is a pipe: it sends one command’s output into the next command as its input. Pipes are what make the command line powerful. Each command does one small job, and you chain them to build exactly the question you want to ask.


Count the values in a column
cut picks out columns: -d , says the columns are separated by commas, and -f 3 asks for the third. Then sort puts identical values next to each other, uniq -c counts each run of identical lines, and sort -rn puts the largest count first:

cut -d , -f 3 bal_baseline.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

    166 Active TB
    153 LTBI
    109 Control
     74 Indeterminate
      1 tb_diagnosis


The header, tb_diagnosis, is counted as a value too. tail -n +2 (everything from line 2 onwards) skips it. Two columns at once count the combinations, here TB diagnosis by HIV status:

tail -n +2 bal_baseline.csv | cut -d , -f 3,4 | sort | uniq -c

    100 Active TB,Negative
     66 Active TB,Positive
     72 Control,Negative
     37 Control,Positive
     44 Indeterminate,Negative
     30 Indeterminate,Positive
     83 LTBI,Negative
     70 LTBI,Positive








Warningcut doesn’t understand quotes



A CSV file can contain commas inside quoted values ("Smith, J"), and cut would split them in the wrong place. This file has no quotes (grep -c '"' bal_baseline.csv prints 0), so cut is safe here. For files that do, use R, Python or a CSV-aware tool such as the ones in Janssens (2021).




Find duplicate IDs
Those two extra rows: uniq -d prints only the lines that appear more than once (again after sort, because uniq only compares neighbouring lines):

tail -n +2 bal_baseline.csv | cut -d , -f 1 | sort | uniq -d

SP09573
SP22251


grep prints every line containing a pattern; -E allows | to mean “or”:

grep -E "SP09573|SP22251" bal_baseline.csv

SP09573,Female,Active TB,Negative,49,2020-10-15,Dr. Jacobs,100,66.6,Right Lower,yolanda,Bloody,3950000,668697,4620000,111,Automated
SP09573,Female,Active TB,Negative,49,2020-10-15,Dr. Jacobs,100,66.6,Right Lower,yolanda,Bloody,3950000,668697,4620000,111,Automated
SP22251,Male,Active TB,Negative,55,2019-06-17,Prof. Malan,80,36.2,Right Upper,fatima,Cream,4730000,1070000,5810000,38,Both
SP22251,Male,Active TB,Negative,55,2019-06-17,Prof. Malan,80,36.2,Right Upper,fatima,Cream,4730000,1070000,5810000,38,Both


Each participant was entered twice, with identical rows. These are the same two duplicates Tutorial 1 finds in R, found here without starting R at all. grep -c counts matching lines instead of printing them:

grep -c "Active TB" bal_baseline.csv

166


grep searches the whole line, not one column, so a pattern can match somewhere you didn’t intend. “Active TB” only appears in the diagnosis column, but a search for a name or a number might not be so tidy. Check with cut first when it matters.


Filter rows on a number
awk can test a column’s value. -F , sets the separator, $16 is the 16th column (time_to_process_min, from the numbered list above), and NR > 1 skips the header. The command prints the ID and processing time of every row where the time is below zero:

awk -F , 'NR > 1 && $16 < 0 {print $1, $16}' bal_baseline.csv

SP24965 -1
SP30729 -1
SP38602 -1


A sample can’t take −1 minutes to process, so these three are recording errors to query. Tutorial 3 deals with impossible measurements like this one when it cleans the data. The same pattern finds the slowest samples, sorting numerically (-n) on column 16:

tail -n +2 bal_baseline.csv | sort -t , -k 16,16 -n | tail -n 3 | cut -d , -f 1,16

SP29084,218
SP08512,248
SP24791,259

title: The command line for biologists
text:
6. Save what you find
> sends a command’s output into a file instead of the screen, and >> adds to the end of a file. Together they can build a smaller CSV with only the active TB participants: the header first, then the matching rows.

head -n 1 bal_baseline.csv > active_tb.csv
grep ",Active TB," bal_baseline.csv >> active_tb.csv
wc -l active_tb.csv

167 active_tb.csv


> replaces the file if it already exists, without asking, so use >> when you mean to add. Searching for ,Active TB, with the commas, rather than plain Active TB, matches the value only when it fills a whole column.
Never write over your raw data: save results to a new file, as here, and keep the original untouched.
